# P-adic differential equations, rigid cohomology and p-adic weights

This roadmap builds the analytic and cohomological library needed to pass from a differential equation near the boundary of a p-adic disc to finite-dimensional cohomology with Frobenius, traces and weights. Its local spine is the algebra of Robba coefficients, variation of differential radii, Frobenius slope filtrations and local monodromy. Its global spine is the theory of overconvergent coefficients, rigid cohomology with its support operations, finiteness and duality, followed by trace formulas, p-adic Weil II and individual Weil factors. The constructions include the interfaces used by Coleman integration, ordinary-locus and Igusa cohomology, and certified point counting.

The targets below specify mathematics to build. A source locator identifies a statement or proof ingredient; it does not turn a proposed target into an existing formal theorem. The [suggested Lean file](../suggested/PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology.lean) states the compact signatures expressible over existing carriers. The analytic rings, coefficient categories and cohomology theories are specified here, with their APIs and discriminating checks. Precise proof and supplier obligations accompany the layers that consume them.

## Scope and boundaries

**Analytic geometry.** AdicSpaces supplies the existing analytic vocabulary. AdicSpacesPartII:F1 owns weak completions, dagger algebras, fringe topology, forms, tensors and localization; R2 owns formal generic fibres and tubes; R3 owns affinoid and quasi-Stein acyclicity. This roadmap builds Robba coefficient theory and Berthelot's overconvergent coefficient/cohomology theory on those objects. Direct-image acyclicity requires quasi-Stein intersections over every target affinoid, not only a Stein source. A partially proper generic-fibre dagger comparison is distinct from the comparison with special-fibre Berthelot rigid cohomology. RD.4 specifies the latter, including its precise model and support data.

**Integral p-adic Hodge theory.** [FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory §§R07.4.7–R07.4.8](../packages/FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory/README.md#r0747-the-robba-ring-and-φ-modules-over-it) supplies the perfect-residue-field case with coefficients W(k)[1/p], q=p and standard Frobenius t↦t^p: its Robba rings, Frobenius modules, slopes, slope filtration and descent of pure modules are imports. RD.0–RD.2 specify the general coefficient and Frobenius-lift theory, including ramified coefficients and the imperfect-residue cases allowed by each target. In the common specialization their carriers, degrees, standard blocks and filtrations must agree. There is one Robba-ring implementation with these compatible specializations. Fontaine–Katz coefficient equivalences likewise retain their stated residue and Frobenius-fixed-field hypotheses.

**Crystalline and logarithmic geometry.** CrystallineCohomology owns crystals, PD envelopes, completed embedding computations and crystalline Frobenius. RD.3 owns the analytic convergent coefficient category and its convergence condition. A topologically quasi-nilpotent connection is not automatically a convergent isocrystal. RD.4 constructs the tube-to-envelope map, its quasi-isomorphism and the constant-coefficient smooth proper comparison; their stable identifiers retain the prefix RD.7. RD.7 packages the coefficient comparison and its linear q-Frobenius normalization. Algebraic log charts, exactification and component residues remain with CrystallineCohomology; analytic log tubes, proper support and their rigid realizations are RD.4 targets. Hyodo–Kato and period-ring comparisons belong to the p-adic comparison roadmaps.

**Local representations and monodromy.** ArithmeticGaloisRepresentations:R01.3 supplies upper ramification groups and Swan conductors, including the required equal-characteristic local fields. RD.2 identifies those conductors with differential breaks. PadicHodgeTheory and PhiGammaModulesAndIwasawaCohomology consume logarithmic local monodromy; their field-of-norms presentation of Berger's rings belongs to the consumer. The theorem here is stated for a supplied finite étale Robba presentation and a compatible unit-multiple derivation. RD.2 owns André's local coefficient category and group; RD.6 owns the neutral Tannakian recognition and global coefficient group, using existing comodule reconstruction where applicable. Lie normalizer and centralizer interfaces belong to ReductiveGroups.

**Finiteness, traces and weights.** AlgebraicCurves supplies algebraic residues and principal parts; RD.5 proves the analytic index comparison for affine curves. LocallyAnalyticDistributions supplies nonarchimedean Hahn–Banach and the requested locally convex/Fredholm theory; RD.5 and RD.6 specify the Robba duality and Dwork-operator applications. OperatorTheory's real/complex Hilbert-space theory does not supply these nonarchimedean LF interfaces. SchemeAndStackFoundations supplies schematic alterations and compactification diagrams; this roadmap supplies the simplicial constructions and rigid cohomological descent. DeligneWeightsAndPurity:DWP.0 supplies eigenvalue weights and determinant/trace algebra; its later layers supply their stated étale purity theorems. RD.6 supplies the rigid trace and weight results. RD.7 exports equality, rationality and integrality of individual Weil factors to WeilConjectures and the all-power point-counting consumers. RD.6–RD.7 own the rationality/Fatou and weight-separation arguments used by the later Weil-factor consumers; DWP.0 supplies their common weights and determinant formalism. A proposed consolidation must preserve this import direction until its ownership change is adopted.

**Applications.** ColemanIntegration imports dagger Frobenius, the affine-curve Monsky–Washnitzer comparison, finiteness and H¹ weights from RD.0, RD.4, RD.5 and RD.6. AutomorphicGaloisRepresentationsPartII:AG2.4 receives a coefficient-specific ordinary-locus comparison, then finite-dimensionality, then weight bounds from RD.4–RD.6. Finite-level Igusa theta quotients have separate construction and finiteness targets; a direct limit of finite-dimensional spaces need not be finite-dimensional. Kloosterman middle rigid cohomology belongs here. Its Galois semistability and weak-admissibility applications also require the proper semistable comparisons of CohomologyComparisons:CP.4; the rigid output alone does not supply them.

## Conventions

Unless a target says otherwise, K is complete discretely valued of characteristic zero, O_K its valuation ring, π a uniformizer and k its residue field of characteristic p. Perfectness, algebraic closure and finiteness of k are separate hypotheses. The Laurent analytic carriers also make sense over general complete nontrivially nonarchimedean fields; every theorem states the additional assumptions it needs. All annular radii are positive. A(r,1) uses convergence at every interior radius r<ρ<1, with decay at both Laurent tails. Its chart topology is Fréchet, and the Robba topology is the locally convex inductive limit. Multiplication is convergent Cauchy convolution. Bounded and integral Robba coefficients differ from the π-adically complete Amice coefficients. On O_E, weak levelwise convergence differs from π-adic convergence. Define these carriers before defining a Frobenius lift; its analytic extension changes the annulus radius.

A connection is linear over the constant field and satisfies Leibniz over the coefficient algebra. A Frobenius structure is an invertible horizontal linearization σ* M→M of a semilinear map, with σ_K reducing to q-power Frobenius, q=p^a. Bijectivity of the semilinear map itself is a separate assertion when σ_K is not onto. Integral Frobenius lattices used for unit-root comparisons require an integral inverse, not only a preserved lattice. The ramified local degree uses v(π)=1: π^c in rank one has slope c and the standard block M_(c,d) has slope c/d. Cohomological q-normalized slopes use v_q=v_p/v_p(q); these conventions are not interchangeable without the normalization factor. Differential breaks concern horizontal convergence and are distinct from Frobenius slopes.

For radius variation write η=e^(−r), order extrinsic subsidiary radii increasingly, and sum the largest negative logarithms. A trivial t-differential line has extrinsic radius η and intrinsic radius one, hence extrinsic profile r and intrinsic profile zero. Coefficient derivations in the multivariable theory must commute and be rational type. Bounded Teichmüller coefficients and their completion are not identified with ordinary Amice coefficients merely because both are denoted E† and E. In the equal-characteristic Hartl–Pink convention φ^r=π^(−d), so arithmetic slope is −d/r while geometric degree is d. The global convergent slope filtration is increasing; the bounded generic descent uses the decreasing arithmetic convention stated at its target.

A frame is X⊂Y⊂P, with X open in Y and Y closed in a formal scheme smooth near X. Properness of Y is an extra compactification assumption. The classical rigid tube uses classical specialization. For a closed T, the adic tube is the interior of its inverse image under continuous specialization. Strict neighborhoods and j† retain their boundary data. Weak fibration gives an open polydisc over a tube. Strong fibration compares cofinal systems of neighborhoods with polydisc radii tending to one: it is not a product with one fixed open unit polydisc over every boundary point. Coherent connections require the Taylor-overconvergence condition; integrability alone does not define an overconvergent coefficient. An invertible horizontal Frobenius forces that condition under the smooth weak-lift hypotheses.

Distinguish ordinary H_rig, compact-support H_c,rig and closed-support H_Z,rig. Log proper support retains the specified proper ambient model X and its open U; impose the support functor on tube sheaves before derived specialization. Its boundary coefficient realization is log convergent. General compact-support base change and pushforward must preserve those supports, not just the underlying de Rham complex. The residue pairing also retains its one-form: for ∂=d/dT use dT, whereas for ∂=(1+T)d/dT use dT/(1+T).

Over F_q, cohomological F is linear q-Frobenius when σ_K=id. Over W(F_q), the p-Frobenius φ is semilinear and φ^a is linear; characteristic polynomials concern that iterate. K(n) multiplies F by q^(−n), lowering weights by 2n. Numerical purity uses an explicitly supplied embedding ι:K^alg→ℂ. A real weight normalization is a constant Frobenius line after the stated coefficient extension, not an integer Tate twist by a real number. Weil factors use P_i(T)=det(1−TF), as in Mathlib's `Matrix.charpolyRev`. A Weil number is algebraic and has the required size at every complex embedding; purity at one ι alone says less.

For Dwork coefficients choose π^(p−1)=−p and ∇e=πe dx, with Frobenius multiplier exp(π(x^q−x)). Its trace is the inverse additive character determined by the splitting-function root. For Kummer coefficients use ∇e=a e dt/t and multiplier t^((q−1)a); the trace uses the corresponding norm character. State p odd where the sign identity needs it. Tate modules are covariant, and geometric Frobenius on étale H¹ is the transpose of arithmetic Frobenius on the Tate module. A row Frobenius matrix records the image of each basis vector in its row: its a-fold twisted product is F^(σ^(a−1))⋯F^σ F. The column convention reverses that order, which affects characteristic polynomials for a≥3.

## Sources

The source spine consists of Kedlaya's local monodromy, slope-filtration, finiteness and p-adic Weil II papers; Berthelot's frame and cohomology constructions; and the curve and functional-analysis work of Crew, Christol–Mebkhout and van der Put. Public proofs of the frame comparisons, weak lifting and proper cohomological descent supply the detailed construction routes below. The register distinguishes source versions; target citations give theorem, section and page locators for the version used. The final proof-obligation sections identify arguments whose source interiors or supplier comparisons still need a precise development. All statements and explanations here are in the roadmap's own words.

<a id="rd0"></a>

## RD.0 — Coefficient rings and analytic foundations

Construct the Laurent, Amice, Cohen/Witt and extended coefficient interfaces, with the topology each comparison uses. Weak substitution precedes analytic Frobenius extension. Valuation p-bases give completed coefficient descent. Controlled weak lifting, fixed-endpoint homotopy and rational integration supply dagger Frobenius independence. Compact preparation and divisor interpolation precede the noncompact Bézout and closed-ideal theorems.

**Landmarks.** Frobenius lift on the Robba ring, Closed ideals and analytic divisors, Bézout property of the Robba ring, Frobenius lift on a dagger algebra, Valuation p-bases, Overconvergent tensor descent.

<a id="target-rd-0-laurent-robba-amice-carriers"></a>

### Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers` · definition

For a complete nontrivially nonarchimedean normed field K, define A(r,1), for 0 < r < 1, by the Laurent coefficient families (a_n) with |a_n|ρ^n tending to zero as |n| tends to infinity for every r < ρ < 1; multiply by convergent Cauchy convolution. Define R_K as their directed union, with each A(r,1) carrying its radius-indexed Fréchet topology and R_K its locally convex inductive-limit topology. Define R^bd by bounded coefficients and R^int by integral coefficients. For the Amice ring E require bounded coefficients and a_n → 0 as n → −∞; O_E is its integral part. These carrier definitions also make sense in equal characteristic; the differential and Frobenius statements below impose their own characteristic hypotheses. For discretely valued K, O_E is the integral part of E, R^bd = R^int[1/π] and E = O_E[1/π]. These are coefficient carriers before a Frobenius lift is chosen; their chart, inductive-limit, valuation and weak topologies are specified separately.

**Hypotheses.**

- K is complete and nontrivially nonarchimedean. The integral and valuation-field assertions additionally require K discretely valued with uniformiser π.
- Every annulus radius is positive; convergence is required at every interior radius, at both Laurent tails.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Robba/Basic`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** `mathlib:DiscreteConvolution.ringConvolution`.

**Sources.**

- [S8](#source-8), Definition 3.5.1, p. 15. Describes the Robba ring as Laurent functions converging on an annulus near the boundary.
- [S1](#source-1), §2.3, pp. 12–14. Distinguishes integral, bounded and completed Laurent coefficients.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- RD.0 analytic topology, weak substitution and coefficient descent: Provides the coefficient families without assuming a Frobenius endomorphism exists.
- RD.1 differential modules; RD.5 relative Robba coefficients: The field coefficient carrier is the starting case; the relative fringe construction is a further target.

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `annulusCoeffs` |  | The K-submodule of coefficient families converging at every positive radius r < ρ < 1, for 0 < r < 1. |
| `robbaCoeffs` |  | The directed union of annulusCoeffs over 0 < r < 1. |
| `RobbaRing` |  | The subtype of robbaCoeffs with convergent Cauchy multiplication and its K-algebra structure. |
| `amiceCoeffs` |  | Bounded coefficient families tending to zero at the negative end. |
| `AmiceRing` |  | The coefficient subtype of amiceCoeffs with its valuation-field structure when K is discretely valued. |
| `gaussNorm` |  | At ρ > 0 where the series converges, sup_n \|a_n\|ρ^n. Outside this domain the total real-valued prototype has no norm interpretation. |
| `RobbaRing.bounded` |  | The bounded-coefficient subring of R_K. |
| `RobbaRing.integral` |  | The subring of R_K with every coefficient of norm at most one. |
| `RobbaRing.coe_mul` |  | Coefficients of multiplication equal convergent discrete convolution, rather than pointwise multiplication. |

**Unit tests.**

- `robba_coordinate_inverse` (computation): The Laurent monomials t and t^−1 multiply to 1.
- `robba_constants_coefficients` (compatibility): The constant series C(c) has coefficient c at 0 and zero at all nonzero indices.
- `robba_negative_tail_nonexample` (non-example): The coefficient family equal to 1 at every negative index and 0 elsewhere belongs neither to R_K nor to E.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Construct the Laurent subalgebras by radius-wise summability of convolution. Positive radii are mandatory. Define restriction, Gauss norms only at radii of convergence, the directed union and its final locally convex topology. This is the coefficient construction of Kedlaya, overview Definition 3.5.1, before the Cohen/Witt comparison. The precise topology and field-extension contracts are laurent-topology-interface and finite-coefficient-extension-interface. Those theorems use these underlying coefficient carriers.
2. Define bounded and integral coefficient subrings and the complete bounded Amice carrier. Multiplication is convergent Cauchy convolution, not pointwise multiplication; the negative-tail condition makes reduction an element of k((t)).

**Checks.**

- The Laurent monomials t and t^−1 multiply to 1.
- The constant series C(c) has coefficient c at 0 and zero at all nonzero indices.
- The coefficient family equal to 1 at every negative index and 0 elsewhere belongs neither to R_K nor to E.
- For perfect k, K=W(k)[1/p], q=p and standard σ(t)=t^p, identify this target with FiniteFlatGroupsAndIntegralPadicHodgeTheory §§R07.4.7–R07.4.8, including its coefficient carriers, degree convention, standard blocks and increasing slope filtration where applicable. This roadmap supplies the stated general coefficient/Frobenius version and its compatibility with that imported special case, rather than a second implementation of the special case.

<a id="target-rd-0-laurent-topology-interface"></a>

### Laurent Fréchet charts and the Robba inductive limit

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/laurent-topology-interface` · construction

On the parent Laurent carrier define A_K(I) for a nonempty interval I of positive multiplicative radii by convergence at every radius in I. At radius ρ use |f|_ρ = sup_n |a_n|ρ^n. On each compact window J=[α,β] inside I use p_J=max(|·|_α,|·|_β). A_K(I) carries the separated complete topology generated by these seminorms and is their compatible projective limit; a compact I gives its Banach norm p_I. For a disc containing the centre use only n≥0 and include evaluation at zero. R_K is the parent union of A_K((r,1)), with the nonarchimedean locally convex inductive-limit topology of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0 (the finest locally convex topology making all chart inclusions continuous); each A_K(I) is the L0 projective limit of its compact-window Banach charts. A cofinal sequence r_j increasing to 1 gives the same locally convex inductive limit (LF) topology. No strictness, bounded-set factorisation or completeness of this inductive limit is assumed.

**Hypotheses.**

- K is complete, nontrivially nonarchimedean, of either characteristic.
- Compact positive-radius annuli may have arbitrary real endpoints; no assumption that the value group is discrete.
- Locally convex is meant in the nonarchimedean sense of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/nonarchimedean-locally-convex-spaces (ultrametric seminorms and open lattices), which rests on the pinned WithSeminorms API rather than on Mathlib’s real convexity predicates. The Gauss seminorms |·|_ρ and p_J are ultrametric.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers](#target-rd-0-laurent-robba-amice-carriers) (`RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers`), `mathlib:WithSeminorms`, `mathlib:WithSeminorms.continuous_of_isBounded`, `LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/nonarchimedean-locally-convex-spaces`, `LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/locally-convex-limits`.

**Sources.**

- [S43](#source-43), §2, (2.1)–(2.6) and Proposition 1, pp.50–51. Laurent series on an interval of valuations, multiplicativity of the Gauss valuation (Proposition 1), the endpoint topology of a closed interval (2.5) and, for a general interval, the coarsest topology making the restrictions to closed subintervals continuous (2.6).
- [S38](#source-38), Definition 2.4.2 and Remark 2.4.3, p.460; Example 2.4.9, p.461. Fréchet completions for the valuations w_s over an interval, their reading as functions on annuli, and the Laurent-series description of the Robba ring.
- [S44](#source-44), Préface §2.5.1, p.24. Fréchet/Banach distinction and locally convex Robba inductive limit.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- RD.1 and parent Frobenius-lift-on-robba-ring: Radius-sensitive continuity of Frobenius pullback.
- Lazard Proposition 10; RD.0 ideal theory: Closure of an ideal is defined in the projective chart topology.
- PadicHodgeTheory:P7 and PhiGammaModulesAndIwasawaCohomology:PG.0: Import these topologies on the one RD.0 coefficient carrier.

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LaurentChart.withSeminorms` |  | The topology is WithSeminorms for the compact-window Gauss family on the parent carrier. |
| `LaurentChart.isNALocallyConvex` |  | Each A_K(I), and R_K, is a Hausdorff nonarchimedean locally convex K-space in the sense of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0 (IsNALocallyConvex): A_K(I) is the L0 projective limit of its compact-window Banach charts and R_K the L0 inductive limit of the charts A_K((r,1)). |
| `LaurentChart.restrict` |  | For J⊆I, restriction A_K(I)→A_K(J) is an injective continuous K-algebra map and composes strictly on coefficients. |
| `LaurentChart.complete` |  | A_K(I) is complete and Hausdorff; the compact endpoint maximum is its Banach norm. |
| `RobbaRing.continuous_linear_iff` |  | A K-linear map from R_K to a nonarchimedean locally convex K-space is continuous iff its restriction to every A_K((r,1)) is continuous; this is the L0 continuity criterion for inductive limits (naInductiveLimit_continuous_iff) applied to the chart system. |
| `RobbaRing.cofinal_charts` |  | Every cofinal countable increasing family r_j→1 yields the same union and the same final seminorm topology. |
| `LaurentChart.mul_bound` |  | p_J(fg)≤p_J(f)p_J(g); constants have Gauss norm \|c\| and \|t^n\|_ρ=ρ^n. |

**Unit tests.**

- `chart_monomial_norm` (computation): On [α,β], p_J(t)=β and p_J(t⁻¹)=α⁻¹; one endpoint cannot replace the maximum.
- `chart_positive_tail` (non-example): Σ_{n≥0}t^n converges on the open unit disc and on every compact subdisc, but not on the closed unit disc.
- `chart_equal_characteristic` (compatibility): For K=F_p((z)), the same annular coefficient conditions and Gauss norms apply; no Witt-vector or characteristic-zero hypothesis enters.
- `disc_centre` (non-example): A chart containing t=0 contains constants and t but excludes t⁻¹; completing Laurent polynomials without excluding negative powers gives the wrong disc.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Use the parent coefficient carrier and convolution. Ultrametric summability gives the submultiplicative Gauss bounds; truncation by finite Laurent polynomials converges on every compact positive-radius window.
2. Construct the compact completion as weighted two-sided null sequences. Compatible coefficient limits on a countable compact exhaustion give completeness and metrisability of A_K(I); the topology does not depend on the exhaustion.
3. For discs use power-series truncations. Give the existing Robba union the locally convex inductive-limit topology of LocallyAnalyticDistributions:L0/locally-convex-limits (i): a lattice is open exactly when its preimage in every chart is open, and a linear map out of R_K is continuous exactly when its restrictions to all charts are. Each chart is the projective limit of part (ii) over its compact windows. Chart restriction is injective and continuous; multiplication is continuous on every fixed chart and separately continuous on the union.

**Checks.**

- Every proposed continuous map must specify its source and target radii.
- Laurent-polynomial density is a chart-topology assertion, not π-adic density in O_E.

<a id="target-rd-0-integral-amice-weak-topology"></a>

### The weak topology on the integral Amice ring

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/integral-amice-weak-topology` · construction

For K a complete discretely valued field with integers O and uniformiser π, give the parent O_E the inverse-limit topology of O_E/π^m≅(O/π^m)((t)), where the latter has the additive t-adic topology: a series is small when every coefficient below a specified index is zero. Thus a fundamental neighbourhood of zero is U(m,N)={f: a_i∈π^m O for all i<N}. Equivalently f_j→0 iff for each m its reduction eventually has t-order tending to +∞. This topology is complete, Hausdorff and a ring topology, and is coarser than the π-adic topology. Finite Laurent polynomials are dense for it. The inverse-limit reductions are ring isomorphisms, not just bijections of coefficient sets.

**Hypotheses.**

- K may have either characteristic; O is a complete DVR.
- The coefficients of every O_E series are integral and tend π-adically to zero towards −∞.
- For each m a reduction has only finitely many negative terms, but may have infinitely many positive terms.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers](#target-rd-0-laurent-robba-amice-carriers) (`RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers`), [Laurent Fréchet charts and the Robba inductive limit](#target-rd-0-laurent-topology-interface) (`RD.0/laurent-topology-interface`).

**Sources.**

- [S38](#source-38), Definition 2.2.7, p.454; Convention 2.3.1 and Definition 2.3.2, p.458. Levelwise topology and the explicit Laurent description. The U(m,N) model is its coefficient-coordinate realisation.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- Parent FrobeniusLift.ofImage and .ext: Convergence and uniqueness are proved in this topology.
- Kedlaya Lemma 2.2.19: The analogous levelwise topology allows extension to completed perfect coefficients.

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AmiceRing.integral_reduce` |  | For every m≥1, O_E/π^m≅(O/π^m)((t)), compatibly with coefficients, multiplication and transition maps. |
| `AmiceRing.weak_nhds_zero` |  | The sets U(m,N), m≥1 and N∈Z, form a neighbourhood basis at zero. |
| `AmiceRing.weak_complete` |  | O_E is complete and separated for the inverse-limit t-adic uniformity. |
| `AmiceRing.laurentPolynomial_weak_dense` |  | Finite Laurent polynomials over O are weak-dense in O_E. |
| `AmiceRing.integralRobba_reduce` |  | R^int/πR^int≅k((t)); surjectivity is obtained by bounded lifts with finitely many negative indices, and the kernel is πR^int. |

**Unit tests.**

- `weak_shift` (computation): t^n→0 weakly as n→∞, but t^n never lies in πO_E, so it does not tend to zero π-adically.
- `weak_geometric_tail` (compatibility): Σ_{i=0}^N t^i converges weakly to (1−t)⁻¹ in O_E; the same sequence is not π-adic Cauchy.
- `weak_negative_tail` (non-example): The family Σ_{i<0}t^i is not in O_E; reduction must be a Laurent series with a finite negative tail.
- `weak_nilpotent_coefficients` (computation): For m=2, reduction is over O/π², not merely over k; πt^N is nonzero there and still tends to zero t-adically.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Reduction of convolution is formal Laurent multiplication because only finitely many summands survive in each coefficient modulo π^m.
2. Choose compatible coefficient lifts in O to identify O_E with the inverse limit of these Laurent series rings. This proves completeness and Hausdorffness of the levelwise topology.
3. The t-adic multiplication estimates on each quotient give the ring topology. Truncate both tails modulo π^m to prove weak density. Every U(m,N) contains π^mO_E, so the identity from the π-adic topology to the weak topology is continuous.

**Checks.**

- Do not use the π-adic completion universal property to justify weak-continuous substitution.

<a id="target-rd-0-weak-substitution-convergence"></a>

### Weak convergence of semilinear Laurent substitution

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/weak-substitution-convergence` · theorem

Let σ_K:K→K be an isometric ring endomorphism preserving O and inducing q-power Frobenius on k, q=p^a with a≥1. For u∈R^int with u≡t^q mod π, the series Σ_i σ_K(a_i)u^i converges in the weak topology for every f=Σ_i a_i t^i∈O_E and defines the unique weak-continuous σ_K-semilinear ring endomorphism with t↦u. Modulo π its action on k((t)) is exactly the q-power map. It is π-adically continuous as well, but weak continuity is essential to its classification.

**Hypotheses.**

- Mixed characteristic for the parent Frobenius object; the weak-convergence lemma itself also applies in equal characteristic when the stated coefficient lift exists.
- u is overconvergent, not an arbitrary unit of O_E, when extending to analytic charts.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [The weak topology on the integral Amice ring](#target-rd-0-integral-amice-weak-topology) (`RD.0/integral-amice-weak-topology`), [Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers](#target-rd-0-laurent-robba-amice-carriers) (`RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers`).

**Sources.**

- [S38](#source-38), Convention 2.3.1 and Definitions 2.2.3, 2.2.7, pp.454,458. Semilinear Frobenius and its levelwise topology; the quotient-wise substitution estimate spells out the convergence behind the displayed substitution.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Modulo π^m write u=t^q(1+h) with h∈π(O/π^m)((t)). The inverse of 1+h is the finite nilpotent geometric sum. Positive powers u^i have t-order at least qi−C_m, since only powers h^j with j<m survive; this estimate is uniform in i.
2. For the positive tail use that estimate, including σ_K on coefficients; for the negative tail a_i vanish modulo π^m once i is sufficiently negative. Thus both tails converge in every quotient.
3. Use finite polynomial substitution and continuity to obtain additivity, multiplicativity and uniqueness on the weak completion. For reduction, raising a Laurent series to q in characteristic p applies q-power to coefficients and multiplies every exponent by q.

**Checks.**

- σ(t⁻¹)=u⁻¹.
- For u=t^q the formula sends a_i t^i to σ_K(a_i)t^{qi}.
- For K=Q_p and u=(1+t)^p−1 the reduction is t^p, although u is not equal to t^p.

<a id="target-rd-0-frobenius-lift-on-robba-ring"></a>

### Weakly continuous Frobenius lifts on the integral Amice ring

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/frobenius-lift-on-robba-ring` · definition

Use the coefficient carriers RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers. Fix K complete discretely valued of characteristic 0 with ring of integers O_K, uniformiser π, residue field k of characteristic p, and a Frobenius lift σ_K on K (a continuous ring endomorphism with σ_K(O_K) ⊆ O_K reducing to x ↦ x^q on k, q = p^a). Let O_E be the ring of Laurent series Σ_{i∈Z} a_i t^i with a_i ∈ O_K and a_i → 0 as i → −∞ (the integral Amice ring; E = O_E[1/π]), let R^int ⊆ O_E be the series converging on some annulus r < |t| < 1 (all coefficients integral), R^bd = R^int[1/π], and R the Robba ring (constructed here from convergent coefficient families, before choosing a Frobenius lift). A Frobenius lift is a ring endomorphism σ of O_E that is σ_K-semilinear on O_K, continuous for the weak (levelwise) topology, and satisfies σ(t) ∈ R^int and σ(t) − t^q ∈ π·R^int. Such σ is determined by u = σ(t) through σ(Σ a_i t^i) = Σ σ_K(a_i) u^i; conversely every u ∈ R^int with u ≡ t^q mod π defines one. Extension to bounded and full Robba rings, with its radius change, is the theorem RD.0/frobenius-radius-comparison; it is not a condition in this definition.

**Hypotheses.**

- K is discretely valued; π is a uniformiser; q = p^a and σ_K induces the q-power map on k. When k is perfect and K = W(k)[1/p], σ_K may be taken to be (a power of) the Witt vector Frobenius.
- The condition σ(t) ∈ R^int is Kedlaya's overconvergence condition lim inf_{i→−∞} w(a_i)/(−i) > 0 on the coefficients of σ(t) (slope filtrations revisited, Convention 2.3.1).
- A Frobenius lift need not be a power of a p-power Frobenius lift (slope filtrations revisited, Remark 2.2.5); the older monodromy paper requires a composition power of a lift of the p-power map.
- No ring of functions on a fixed annulus r < |t| < 1 carries a Frobenius lift: σ moves the inner radius from r to r^{1/q}.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Robba/FrobeniusLift`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers](#target-rd-0-laurent-robba-amice-carriers) (`RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers`), [The weak topology on the integral Amice ring](#target-rd-0-integral-amice-weak-topology) (`RD.0/integral-amice-weak-topology`), [Weak convergence of semilinear Laurent substitution](#target-rd-0-weak-substitution-convergence) (`RD.0/weak-substitution-convergence`), `mathlib:WittVector.frobenius`.

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.2.3 and Remark 2.2.5, p. 8. The definition of a Frobenius lift, with q = p^a and no requirement to be a power of a p-power lift.
- [S2](#source-2), Convention 2.3.1, pp. 11-12. The overconvergence condition σ(t) ∈ R^int on the image of the coordinate.
- [S1](#source-1), Section 1.1, p. 3. Why the lift lives on the Robba ring and not on a fixed annulus (the radius statement is recorded with its misprint corrected in sourceIssues).
- [S1](#source-1), Section 2.3, p. 12. Uniqueness of the lift given σ(t).

**Uses and API requirements.**

- Kedlaya, slope filtrations revisited, Definition 3.1.1: σ-modules over Γ_an,con are defined relative to a chosen Frobenius lift
- Kedlaya, A p-adic local monodromy theorem, Theorem 1.1: the local monodromy theorem is asserted for any Frobenius for the Robba ring
- Kedlaya, local monodromy overview, Definitions 6.1.1-6.1.2: a Frobenius structure on a ∇-module is an isomorphism with its pullback along a Frobenius lift
- RD.1 Frobenius modules and (φ,∇)-modules; RD.2 slope filtration and local monodromy: all Frobenius structures over R, R^bd, E are relative to such σ
- PhiGammaModulesAndIwasawaCohomology:PG.0 and PadicHodgeTheory:P7: the cyclotomic φ(t) = (1+t)^p − 1 is an instance
- Robba coefficients for cyclotomic p-adic Hodge consumers: RD.0 exports the single general Laurent-series carrier; P7 and its cyclotomic consumers import it. Import the integral perfect-Witt/standard-Frobenius specialization and extend its compatible coefficient theory.

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift` |  | A Frobenius lift: σ_K on K together with u = σ(t) ∈ R^int with u − t^q ∈ π·R^int; the ring endomorphism of O_E it induces. |
| `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.ofImage` |  | For u ∈ R^int with u ≡ t^q mod π there is a unique Frobenius lift with σ(t) = u. |
| `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.ext` |  | Two Frobenius lifts with the same σ_K and the same image of t are equal. |
| `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.standard` |  | The standard lift σ(t) = t^q, σ(Σ a_i t^i) = Σ σ_K(a_i) t^{qi}. |
| `RobbaRing.FrobeniusLift.reduction` |  | Modulo π, the weakly continuous lift on O_E induces q-power Frobenius on O_E/πO_E = k((t)). Preservation and reduction of R^int are consequences of RD.0/frobenius-radius-comparison. |

**Unit tests.**

- `frobeniusLift_standard_apply` (computation): For the standard lift and f = Σ a_i t^i in O_E: σ(f) = Σ σ_K(a_i) t^{qi}; in particular σ(t^{-1}) = t^{-q}.
- `frobeniusLift_reduction` (compatibility): The reduction of σ modulo π on O_E/πO_E = k((t)) is x ↦ x^q.
- `frobeniusLift_ext_image` (characterisation): If σ, σ' are Frobenius lifts with σ_K = σ'_K and σ(t) = σ'(t) then σ = σ' on O_E.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Existence and uniqueness from u: O_E is the π-adic completion of O_K[[t]][t^{-1}]; Laurent polynomials are dense for the weak levelwise topology, which is different from the π-adic topology (monodromy paper, Section 2.3), so a levelwise-continuous σ is determined by σ(t) and σ_K; u is a unit of O_E because its reduction t^q is a unit of k((t)), so Σ σ_K(a_i) u^i converges levelwise.
2. Use RD.0/integral-amice-weak-topology and RD.0/weak-substitution-convergence for the existence, uniqueness and reduction assertions. The extension theorem uses this lift after constructing the analytic comparison, and is not a prerequisite of the lift definition.

**Checks.**

- For the standard lift and f = Σ a_i t^i in O_E: σ(f) = Σ σ_K(a_i) t^{qi}; in particular σ(t^{-1}) = t^{-q}.
- The reduction of σ modulo π on R^int/πR^int = k((t)) is x ↦ x^q.
- Analytic extension and the cyclotomic logarithm identity are checked in RD.0/frobenius-radius-comparison.

<a id="target-rd-0-witt-partial-valuations"></a>

### Partial valuations v_n, w_r on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors W_con

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/witt-partial-valuations` · definition

Let ℓ be a perfect field of characteristic p with a (possibly trivial) valuation v_ℓ, complete, let k_0 ⊆ ℓ be a perfect subfield on which v_ℓ is trivial, and let O be a finite totally ramified extension of W(k_0) with uniformiser π, equipped with an extension of σ; put W(ℓ, O) = W(ℓ) ⊗_{W(k_0)} O. Every x ∈ W(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] has a unique Teichmüller expansion x = Σ_{i∈Z} [z_i] π^i (z_i ∈ ℓ, zero for i ≪ 0). For n ∈ Z put v_n(x) = min_{i ≤ n} v_ℓ(z_i); for r > 0 put v_{n,r}(x) = r·v_n(x) + n; at r = 0 set v_{n,0}(x) = n when v_n(x) is finite and ∞ otherwise, let W_r(ℓ, O) be the set of x ∈ W(ℓ, O) with v_{n,r}(x) → ∞ as n → ∞, and w_r(x) = min_n v_{n,r}(x); w = w_0 is the π-adic valuation normalised by w(π) = 1. Put W_con(ℓ, O) = ∪_{r>0} W_r(ℓ, O).

**Hypotheses.**

- ℓ perfect and complete for v_ℓ; the valuation may be trivial, in which case W_r = W and W_con = W(ℓ, O).
- Normalisation w(π) = 1 (Kedlaya, slope filtrations revisited, Remark 2.1.11), not w(p) = 1; results do not depend on it.
- σ on W(ℓ, O) is the log_p(q)-th power of the Witt vector Frobenius σ_0, tensored with the given σ on O; then v_n(x^σ) = q·v_n(x) and w_r(x) = w_{r/q}(x^σ).

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Robba/WittPartial`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** `mathlib:WittVector`, `mathlib:WittVector.teichmuller`, `mathlib:WittVector.frobenius`, `mathlib:AddValuation`.

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.1.4, p. 6. Teichmüller expansions.
- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.1.5, p. 6. The rings W_r and the effect of σ.
- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.1.8, p. 7. W_con and its basic structure.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- Kedlaya, slope filtrations revisited, Sections 2.1-2.4: the analytic rings Γ_I and Γ_an,con are completions of W_r[π^{-1}] for the w_s
- RD.0 extended Robba ring: R^alg is built from W(ℓ̂^alg, O) with these valuations
- RD.1 eigenvector and Dieudonné-Manin arguments: all estimates are phrased with v_n, v_{n,r}, w_r

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WittPartial.v` |  | The partial valuation v_n(x) = min_{i ≤ n} v_ℓ(z_i) on W(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}], valued in R ∪ {∞}. |
| `WittPartial.w` |  | w_r(x) = min_n v_{n,r}(x); at r = 0 use the separately defined v_{n,0}, so w_0 is the π-adic valuation. |
| `WittPartial.overconvergentSubring` |  | The subring W_r(ℓ, O) of x with v_{n,r}(x) → ∞ as n → ∞, and W_con = ∪_r W_r. |
| `WittPartial.v_add` |  | v_n(x + y) ≥ min(v_n(x), v_n(y)), with equality if the minimum is attained once. |
| `WittPartial.v_mul` |  | v_n(xy) ≥ min_m (v_m(x) + v_{n−m}(y)), with equality if the minimum is attained once. |
| `WittPartial.v_frobenius` |  | v_n(x^σ) = q·v_n(x); hence w_r(x) = w_{r/q}(x^σ). |
| `WittPartial.v_teichmuller` |  | v_n([z]) = v_ℓ(z) for n ≥ 0 and z ∈ ℓ. |

**Unit tests.**

- `wittPartial_v_teichmuller` (computation): For z ∈ ℓ nonzero: v_n([z]) = v_ℓ(z) for all n ≥ 0 and v_n([z]) = ∞ for n < 0.
- `wittPartial_w_pi` (computation): w_r(π) = 1; for z ≠ 0, w_r([z]) = r·v_ℓ(z) for r ≥ 0; w_r(0) = ∞.
- `wittPartial_trivial_valuation` (degenerate): If v_ℓ is trivial then W_r(ℓ, O) = W(ℓ, O) for all r ≥ 0 and w_r = w.
- `wittPartial_compat_mathlib_witt` (compatibility): For O = W(k_0) and π = p, W(ℓ, O) is Mathlib's WittVector p ℓ and the Teichmüller lift is WittVector.teichmuller.
- `wittPartial_not_overconvergent` (non-example): If y ∈ ℓ has v_ℓ(y) < 0, the element x = Σ_{i≥0} [y^{q^i}] π^i of W(ℓ, O) satisfies v_{n,r}(x) = r q^n v_ℓ(y) + n → −∞, so x lies in no W_r(ℓ, O) with r > 0.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Existence and uniqueness of Teichmüller expansions: each x ∈ W(ℓ, O) is uniquely Σ_{i≥0} [z_i] π^i (slope filtrations revisited, Definition 2.1.4); inverting π allows finitely many negative i.
2. The inequalities v_n(x + y) ≥ min(v_n(x), v_n(y)), v_n(xy) ≥ min_m (v_m(x) + v_{n−m}(y)) with equality when the minimum is attained once, v_n(x^σ) = q v_n(x) and v_n([z]) = v_ℓ(z) for n ≥ 0 follow from the Witt vector addition and multiplication formulas (Definition 2.1.5).
3. σ sends W_{qr} onto W_r (Definition 2.1.5); W_r is a subring by the inequalities.

**Checks.**

- For ℓ with trivial valuation W_r(ℓ, O) = W(ℓ, O) for every r.
- For z ∈ ℓ with v_ℓ(z) > 0 the Teichmüller lift [z] lies in every W_r and is a unit in W_r if z ≠ 0 (Remark 2.2.11(a)).
- If v_ℓ(y) < 0, then Σ_{i≥0} [y^{q^i}] π^i lies in W(ℓ, O) but in no W_r(ℓ, O).

<a id="target-rd-0-partial-valuation-multiplicativity"></a>

### w_r is a valuation on W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] (Newton-polygon additivity)

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/partial-valuation-multiplicativity` · lemma

For x, y ∈ W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] nonzero, let i, j be the smallest and largest n achieving min_n v_{n,r}(x), and k, l those for y. Then i + k and j + l are the smallest and largest n achieving min_n v_{n,r}(xy), and w_r(xy) = w_r(x) + w_r(y). In particular w_r is a valuation on W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] and w_r(x) = w_{r/q}(x^σ).

**Hypotheses.**

- ℓ perfect, complete for v_ℓ; notation of the partial-valuation node.

**Prerequisites.** [Partial valuations v_n, w_r on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors W_con](#target-rd-0-witt-partial-valuations) (`RD.0/witt-partial-valuations`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Lemma 2.1.7 and Definition 2.1.8, pp. 6-7. Exactly the statement.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Apply v_{m,r}(xy) ≥ min_n (v_{n,r}(x) + v_{m−n,r}(y)) with equality when the minimum is attained once.
2. For m = i + k and m = j + l the value v_{i,r}(x) + v_{k,r}(y) is attained exactly once; for m < i + k or m > j + l it is never attained; this gives the claim.

**Checks.**

- Rank one check: w_r([z]π^m) = r v_ℓ(z) + m and the product rule holds on monomials.

<a id="target-rd-0-overconvergent-witt-vectors-henselian"></a>

### W_con(ℓ, O) is a henselian discrete valuation ring

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/overconvergent-witt-vectors-henselian` · lemma

W_con(ℓ, O) is a discrete valuation ring with maximal ideal (π) and residue field ℓ; it is henselian, and it is not π-adically complete when v_ℓ is nontrivial.

**Hypotheses.**

- ℓ perfect and complete for v_ℓ.

**Prerequisites.** [Partial valuations v_n, w_r on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors W_con](#target-rd-0-witt-partial-valuations) (`RD.0/witt-partial-valuations`), [w_r is a valuation on W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] (Newton-polygon additivity)](#target-rd-0-partial-valuation-multiplicativity) (`RD.0/partial-valuation-multiplicativity`), `mathlib:HenselianLocalRing`, `mathlib:IsDiscreteValuationRing`.

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Lemma 2.1.12, p. 7. The statement.
- [S2](#source-2), Proof of Lemma 2.1.12, p. 7. The proof outline.

**Construction or proof.**

1. DVR: every nonzero x ∈ W_con is π^m times an element with nonzero reduction; an element of W_r with nonzero reduction u_0 is a unit in some W_s (Remark 2.1.10: u is a unit of W_r iff v_{n,r}(u) > v_{0,r}(u) for n > 0, which holds after shrinking r).
2. Henselian: given a polynomial P over W_con and y with P(y) ≡ 0 and P'(y) ≢ 0 mod π, choose r with w_r(P(y)/P'(y)) > 0; Newton iteration converges both for w and for w_r, so the root lies in W_r (Lemma 2.1.12).
3. Non-completeness: see the non-example of the partial-valuation node.

**Checks.**

- The residue map W_con → ℓ is surjective (Teichmüller lifts) with kernel πW_con.
- Hensel test: for p odd and ℓ ∋ y with y^2 = c, the polynomial X^2 − [c] has a root in W_con lifting y.

<a id="target-rd-0-analytic-ring"></a>

### Kedlaya's analytic rings Γ^ℓ_I, Γ^ℓ_an,r and Γ^ℓ_an,con

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/analytic-ring` · construction

Let ℓ be a field of characteristic p complete for a (possibly trivial) valuation v_ℓ, k_0 ⊆ ℓ a subfield on which v_ℓ is trivial, O finite totally ramified over the Cohen ring C_{k_0} with uniformiser π, Γ = Γ^ℓ = C_ℓ ⊗_{C_{k_0}} O, and σ a Frobenius lift on Γ (lifting the q-power map of ℓ) carrying O into itself. Via the completed direct limit of Γ →σ Γ →σ ⋯ ≅ W(ℓ^perf, O^perf) the functions v_n, v_{n,r}, w_r restrict to Γ; put Γ_r = Γ ∩ W_r(ℓ^perf, O). Say Γ has enough r_0-units if every nonzero element of ℓ lifts to a unit of Γ_{r_0}, and assume this. For I ⊆ [0, r_0) bounded away from r_0, Γ_I is the Fréchet completion of Γ_{r_0}[π^{-1}] for the valuations w_s, s ∈ I; Γ_an,r = Γ_{(0,r]}, Γ_an,con = ∪_{r<r_0} Γ_an,r, Γ_con = ∪ Γ_r (a henselian DVR). σ induces Γ_I → Γ_{q^{-1}I}; for I ⊆ J the restriction Γ_J → Γ_I is injective with dense image. The Newton polygon of x ∈ Γ_I is the lower convex hull of the points (v_n(x), n) with the segments of slope −s, s ∉ I, removed; its slopes (with multiplicities) are the slopes of x.

**Hypotheses.**

- ℓ complete; 'enough r_0-units' holds for ℓ perfect (Teichmüller lifts) and for ℓ = k((t)) by the comparison of naive and true valuations (see the Robba ring comparison node) and it passes to finite separable extensions.
- When v_ℓ is trivial, Γ_an,con = Γ_con[π^{-1}] = Γ[π^{-1}] is a complete discretely valued field.
- Kedlaya's K is written ℓ here, to keep K for the characteristic-0 coefficient field.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Robba/AnalyticRing`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Partial valuations v_n, w_r on Witt vectors and the overconvergent Witt vectors W_con](#target-rd-0-witt-partial-valuations) (`RD.0/witt-partial-valuations`), [w_r is a valuation on W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] (Newton-polygon additivity)](#target-rd-0-partial-valuation-multiplicativity) (`RD.0/partial-valuation-multiplicativity`), [W_con(ℓ, O) is a henselian discrete valuation ring](#target-rd-0-overconvergent-witt-vectors-henselian) (`RD.0/overconvergent-witt-vectors-henselian`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.2.3, p. 8. How the valuations reach Γ.
- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.2.10, p. 8. The 'enough units' hypothesis.
- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.4.2, p. 14. The rings Γ_I.
- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.4.8, p. 15. The ring Γ_an,con.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- Kedlaya, slope filtrations revisited, Chapters 3-6: σ-modules, Harder-Narasimhan filtrations and Dieudonné-Manin decompositions live over Γ_an,con
- RD.0 Robba ring comparison: for ℓ = k((t)) this is the Robba ring with its Frobenius lift
- RD.0 extended Robba ring: for ℓ the completed algebraic closure of k((t)) this is R^alg
- RD.2 slope filtration and descent (Kedlaya Chapter 6): descent runs along Γ^L_an,con for finite separable L

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AnalyticRing.intervalRing` |  | Γ_I for I ⊆ [0, r_0) bounded away from r_0: the Fréchet completion of Γ_{r_0}[π^{-1}] for (w_s)_{s∈I}. |
| `AnalyticRing.analyticRing` |  | Γ_an,r = Γ_{(0,r]} and Γ_an,con = ∪_{r} Γ_an,r, with its limit-of-Fréchet topology. |
| `AnalyticRing.boundedSubring` |  | Γ_con = ∪_r Γ_r, a henselian DVR with residue field ℓ, and Γ_con[π^{-1}] ⊆ Γ_an,con. |
| `AnalyticRing.restrict` |  | For I ⊆ J the injective restriction Γ_J → Γ_I with dense image. |
| `AnalyticRing.frobenius` |  | σ: Γ_I → Γ_{q^{-1}I}, compatible with restriction. |
| `AnalyticRing.slopes` |  | The Newton polygon and slope multiset of x ∈ Γ_I (slopes in I, finite multiplicity; for x ∈ Γ_an,r the slopes decrease to 0). |
| `AnalyticRing.isDomain` |  | Γ_I and Γ_an,con are integral domains. |
| `AnalyticRing.trivialValuation` |  | If v_ℓ is trivial then Γ_an,con = Γ[π^{-1}]. |

**Unit tests.**

- `analyticRing_trivial_valuation` (degenerate): If v_ℓ is trivial, Γ_an,con = Γ[π^{-1}] and every nonzero element is a unit.
- `analyticRing_closed_interval` (computation): For I = [0, s], Γ_I = Γ_s[π^{-1}].
- `analyticRing_slopes_monomial` (computation): For ℓ = k((t)), O = W(k) and the standard lift, the Laurent polynomial t − p has exactly one slope, equal to 1 with multiplicity 1 (its zero lies on |t| = |π|^1), while u·π^m for a unit u of Γ_{r_0} has no slopes.
- `analyticRing_compat_robba` (compatibility): For ℓ = k((t)) and a Frobenius lift with σ(t) overconvergent, Γ_an,con coincides with the Robba ring constructed in the Frobenius-lift node (see the comparison node).
- `analyticRing_not_noetherian` (non-example): For ℓ = k((t)) the ideal generated by x_j = Π_{i ≥ j}(1 − u^{p^i}/p^i), j ≥ 1, is not finitely generated, so Γ_an,con is not noetherian.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Definitions 2.2.1-2.2.13 of slope filtrations revisited: Cohen ring, Frobenius lift, embedding into W(ℓ^perf, O^perf), Γ_r, enough units, Γ_con.
2. Definition 2.4.2: Fréchet completion Γ_I; the functions v_n, v_{n,s}, w_s extend by continuity; σ: Γ_I → Γ_{q^{-1}I}; restriction maps injective with dense image (density of Γ_{r_0}[π^{-1}]).
3. Definition 2.4.4 (Newton polygon of elements) and Definition 2.4.8 (Γ_an,con).
4. Γ_con is a henselian DVR with residue field ℓ: Definition 2.2.13 with Lemma 2.1.12 applied inside W_con(ℓ^perf, O).

**Checks.**

- For ℓ with trivial valuation: Γ_I = Γ[π^{-1}] for every I and Γ_an,con = Γ[π^{-1}].
- For I = [0, s]: Γ_I = Γ_s[π^{-1}].
- For ℓ = k((t)): Γ_an,con is the Robba ring (comparison node).

<a id="target-rd-0-analytic-ring-slope-additivity"></a>

### Slopes of a product are the sums of the slopes; Γ_I is a domain

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/analytic-ring-slope-additivity` · lemma

For x, y ∈ Γ_I nonzero and s ∈ I, the multiplicity of s as a slope of xy is the sum of its multiplicities as a slope of x and of y. In particular Γ_I and Γ_an,con are integral domains. For a closed interval [r', r] ⊆ [0, r_0) the total multiplicity of x ∈ Γ_{[r',r]} is finite and equals i − j, where i is the largest n achieving min_n v_{n,r}(x) and j the smallest n achieving min_n v_{n,r'}(x).

**Hypotheses.**

- Notation of the analytic-ring construction.

**Prerequisites.** [Kedlaya's analytic rings Γ^ℓ_I, Γ^ℓ_an,r and Γ^ℓ_an,con](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring) (`RD.0/analytic-ring`), [w_r is a valuation on W_r(ℓ, O)[π^{-1}] (Newton-polygon additivity)](#target-rd-0-partial-valuation-multiplicativity) (`RD.0/partial-valuation-multiplicativity`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Lemma 2.4.7, p. 15. The statement.
- [S2](#source-2), Remark 2.4.6, p. 15. Finiteness of total multiplicity.

**Construction or proof.**

1. For x, y ∈ Γ_r[π^{-1}] this is the multiplicativity lemma for w_r applied at each s ∈ I.
2. In general approximate x, y in Γ_I by elements of Γ_r[π^{-1}] closely enough that the extremal indices are unchanged (Lemma 2.4.7).
3. Finiteness of total multiplicity: Remark 2.4.6.

**Checks.**

- For elements of O[π^{-1}]^× there are no slopes; a product of two elements each with one slope s of multiplicity 1 has slope s with multiplicity 2.

<a id="target-rd-0-semiunit-presentation"></a>

### Semiunit presentations of elements of Γ_I

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/semiunit-presentation` · lemma

Call a semiunit an element of Γ_{r_0} that is zero or a unit. For I ⊆ [0, r_0) bounded away from r_0, every x ∈ Γ_I admits a semiunit presentation x = Σ_{i∈Z} u_i π^i (u_i semiunits, the sum converging in Γ_I). For any semiunits u_i and r ∈ (0, r_0), w_r(u_i π^i) ≥ min_{n≤i} v_{n,r}(Σ_{j≤i} u_j π^j).

**Hypotheses.**

- Γ has enough r_0-units (this is what makes each residue class liftable to a semiunit).

**Prerequisites.** [Kedlaya's analytic rings Γ^ℓ_I, Γ^ℓ_an,r and Γ^ℓ_an,con](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring) (`RD.0/analytic-ring`), [Slopes of a product are the sums of the slopes; Γ_I is a domain](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring-slope-additivity) (`RD.0/analytic-ring-slope-additivity`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.5.2 and Proposition 2.5.5, pp. 16-18. The statement.
- [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.5.2, p. 16. Definition of semiunit.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Lemma 2.5.3(a),(b): estimates for partial sums of semiunit series, by induction on i.
2. Lemma 2.5.4: a semiunit presentation over Γ_{[r,r]} of an element with v_{n,s}(x) → ∞ for s ∈ I converges in Γ_I.
3. Proposition 2.5.5: first for x ∈ Γ_r by successive π-adic approximation with semiunits; then for I = [r,r] by approximating x by elements x_l ∈ Γ_r[π^{-1}] and correcting finitely many terms at each stage; the corrections for a fixed i form a series converging in Γ_{r_0} whose limit is a semiunit; the general I follows from Lemma 2.5.4.

**Checks.**

- If ℓ is perfect, the Teichmüller presentation Σ [f_n(x)] π^n is a semiunit presentation.

<a id="target-rd-0-analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections"></a>

### Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for Γ_I

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections` · lemma

(a) For r ∈ (0, r_0) and x ∈ Γ_{[r,r]}: x ∈ Γ_r iff v_n(x) = ∞ for all n < 0. (b) For I ⊆ J bounded away from r_0 and x ∈ Γ_I with v_{n,s}(x) → ∞ as n → ±∞ for every s ∈ J: x ∈ Γ_J. (c) For ℓ ⊆ ℓ' complete, Γ^ℓ and Γ^{ℓ'} having enough r_0-units, and I ⊆ J ⊆ [0, r_0) bounded away from r_0: Γ^ℓ_I ∩ Γ^{ℓ'}_J = Γ^ℓ_J inside Γ^{ℓ'}_I; in particular Γ^ℓ[π^{-1}] ∩ Γ^{ℓ'}_con[π^{-1}] = Γ^ℓ_con[π^{-1}]. (d) For I = [a,b], J = [c,d] with a ≤ c ≤ b ≤ d: Γ_I ∩ Γ_J = Γ_{I∪J} inside Γ_{I∩J}, and every x ∈ Γ_{I∩J} with w_s(x) > 0 on I∩J splits as y + z, y ∈ Γ_I, z ∈ Γ_J, with w_s(y) ≥ (s/c)w_c(x) on [a,c], w_s(z) ≥ (s/b)w_b(x) on [b,d], min(w_s(y), w_s(z)) ≥ w_s(x) on [c,b]. (e) For I closed ⊆ [0,r] and x ∈ Γ_I, assume r ∈ I or that min_{n<0} v_{n,s}(x) is finite for every s ∈ I. Then there is y ∈ Γ_r with w_s(x − y) ≥ min_{n<0} v_{n,s}(x) for s ∈ I.

**Hypotheses.**

- Enough r_0-units for all rings involved.

**Prerequisites.** [Semiunit presentations of elements of Γ_I](#target-rd-0-semiunit-presentation) (`RD.0/semiunit-presentation`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Corollary 2.5.6, p. 18. Part (a).
- [S2](#source-2), Corollary 2.5.8, p. 19. Part (c).
- [S2](#source-2), Corollary 2.5.9, p. 19. Part (d).
- [S2](#source-2), Proof of Theorem 5.5.2, p. 59. The intersection statement in the form used downstream.

**Construction or proof.**

1. (a) Corollary 2.5.6 from a semiunit presentation: a nonzero u_j, j < 0, would give v_{j}(x) < ∞.
2. (b) Corollary 2.5.7: take a semiunit presentation over Γ_I and apply Lemma 2.5.4.
3. (c) Corollary 2.5.8 from (b); the special case with I = [0,0] and J = [0,s], s → 0, gives the intersection statement used in the comparison of generic and special polygons.
4. (d) Corollary 2.5.9: split a semiunit presentation into the parts with i ≤ 0 and i > 0.
5. (e) Lemma 2.5.11: truncate a semiunit presentation.

**Checks.**

- For ℓ = k((t)) and x a Laurent series in the Robba ring: (a) says a function bounded on a closed circle whose negative partial valuations vanish is a power series in the bounded ring; (c) gives E ∩ R^int_alg-type intersections.

<a id="target-rd-0-units-of-analytic-ring"></a>

### Units of Γ_I are the elements without slopes; units of Γ_an,r lie in Γ_r[π^{-1}]

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/units-of-analytic-ring` · theorem

A nonzero x ∈ Γ_I is a unit of Γ_I iff it has no slopes (in I). If I = (0, r], this holds iff x is a unit of Γ_r[π^{-1}]. Consequently the units of Γ_an,con are exactly the units of Γ_con[π^{-1}], i.e. the nonzero elements of the field Γ_con[π^{-1}].

**Hypotheses.**

- Enough r_0-units.
- Γ_con is a DVR, so Γ_con[π^{-1}] is its fraction field.

**Prerequisites.** [Slopes of a product are the sums of the slopes; Γ_I is a domain](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring-slope-additivity) (`RD.0/analytic-ring-slope-additivity`), [Semiunit presentations of elements of Γ_I](#target-rd-0-semiunit-presentation) (`RD.0/semiunit-presentation`), [Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for Γ_I](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections) (`RD.0/analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Corollary 2.5.12, p. 19. The statement.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Units have no slopes by slope additivity.
2. Conversely if x has no slopes, one index m minimises v_{m,s}(x) for all s ∈ I; normalise m = 0; the truncation lemma (e) gives y ∈ Γ_r close to x, and enough units gives a unit z of Γ_r with w(y − z) > 0; then w_s(1 − x z^{-1}) > 0 on I and Σ (1 − x z^{-1})^i converges to (x z^{-1})^{-1}.
3. For I = (0, r]: no slopes forces v_n(x) = ∞ for n < m, so x ∈ Γ_r[π^{-1}] by the membership criterion, and likewise x^{-1}.

**Checks.**

- π and the units of O are units; for ℓ = k((t)) the element Π_{i≥1}(1 − t^{p^i}/p^i) of R has infinitely many slopes and is not a unit (monodromy paper, Section 2.3).

<a id="target-rd-0-closed-interval-analytic-ring-pid"></a>

### Γ_r and Γ_I for closed I are principal ideal domains (Lazard)

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/closed-interval-analytic-ring-pid` · theorem

For r ∈ (0, r_0), Γ_r is a principal ideal domain, and for every closed interval I ⊆ [0, r_0), Γ_I is a principal ideal domain. For ℓ = k((t)) these are the rings of bounded functions on |π|^r ≤ |t| < 1 and of analytic functions on the closed annulus {log_{|π|}|t| ∈ I}, and the statement specialises to Lazard's theorem.

**Hypotheses.**

- O is a complete discretely valued coefficient ring with uniformiser π; the valuation on ℓ need not be discrete.
- Enough r_0-units.

**Prerequisites.** [Semiunit presentations of elements of Γ_I](#target-rd-0-semiunit-presentation) (`RD.0/semiunit-presentation`), [Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for Γ_I](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections) (`RD.0/analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections`), [Units of Γ_I are the elements without slopes; units of Γ_an,r lie in Γ_r[π^{-1}]](#target-rd-0-units-of-analytic-ring) (`RD.0/units-of-analytic-ring`), `mathlib:IsPrincipalIdealRing`.

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Proposition 2.6.5, p. 21. First statement.
- [S2](#source-2), Proposition 2.6.8, p. 22. Second statement.
- [S2](#source-2), Remark 2.6.4, p. 21. Why discreteness is a hypothesis.
- [S8](#source-8), Proposition 3.2.3, p. 11. Lazard's form for closed annuli.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Positioning (Lemma 2.6.1): for x ∈ Γ_{[r,r]} nonzero there are a unit u of Γ_{r_0} and i with uπ^i x normalised (w_r = 0, v_0(· − 1) > 0, v_{n,r} > 0 for n < 0).
2. Division algorithm (Lemma 2.6.3): define the height of x ∈ Γ_r; for x ≠ 0 and y there is z of smaller height with y − z ∈ xΓ_r and w_r(z) ≥ w_r(y); use a positive contraction bound on each closed subinterval and induct over the finite set of critical valuation indices, as in the corrected proof of Lemma 2.6.3.
3. Γ_r is a PID (Proposition 2.6.5): an element of minimal height generates any nonzero ideal.
4. Factorisation (Lemma 2.6.7): for I = [r', r] and x ∈ Γ_I there is a unit u of Γ_I with ux ∈ Γ_r having all slopes in I.
5. Γ_I is a PID (Proposition 2.6.8): the ideal of Γ_r generated by the ux, x ∈ J, is principal by Proposition 2.6.5 (the printed proof cites 2.6.8 itself; see sourceIssues) and its generator generates J.

**Checks.**

- Γ_{[0,0]} = Γ[π^{-1}] is a field (a PID trivially).
- For ℓ = k((t)) and I = [s,s] a single circle, every ideal of the ring of analytic functions on the circle is generated by a polynomial (Lazard; overview Proposition 3.2.3).

<a id="target-rd-0-matrix-approximation-and-factorization"></a>

### Approximation of invertible matrices and factorisation over overlapping intervals

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/matrix-approximation-and-factorization` · lemma

(a) For I closed ⊆ [0, r], r < r_0, and M ∈ GL_n(Γ_I) there is U ∈ GL_n(Γ_r[π^{-1}]) with w_s(MU − I_n) > 0 for s ∈ I; if w_s(det M − 1) > 0 on I one can take det U = 1. (b) For I = [a,b], J = [c,d] with a ≤ c ≤ b ≤ d and M an n×n matrix over Γ_{I∩J} with w_s(M − I_n) > 0 on I∩J, there are U ∈ GL_n(Γ_I), V ∈ GL_n(Γ_J) with M = UV.

**Hypotheses.**

- Enough r_0-units; O is complete discretely valued as in the corrected PID node.

**Prerequisites.** [Γ_r and Γ_I for closed I are principal ideal domains (Lazard)](#target-rd-0-closed-interval-analytic-ring-pid) (`RD.0/closed-interval-analytic-ring-pid`), [Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for Γ_I](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections) (`RD.0/analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Lemma 2.7.1, p. 23. Part (a).
- [S2](#source-2), Lemma 2.7.2, p. 25. Part (b).

**Construction or proof.**

1. (a) Lemma 2.7.1: induction on n; choose the last row of a determinant-one matrix A over the PID Γ_r[π^{-1}] approximating the cofactor relation, using that β_n' + c for c ∈ O of large valuation are pairwise coprime; then approximate Gaussian elimination and back-substitution over Γ_I, and approximate the elementary factors over Γ_r.
2. (b) Lemma 2.7.2: iterate M_l = U_l^{-1} M V_l^{-1}, splitting M_l − I_n = Y_l + Z_l by the Mayer-Vietoris splitting (intersections node (d)); the products converge and the estimates put the limits in GL_n(Γ_I) and GL_n(Γ_J).

**Checks.**

- n = 1: (a) is the positioning lemma; (b) is the additive splitting followed by exponentiation-free iteration.

<a id="target-rd-0-vector-bundles-on-half-open-intervals-free"></a>

### Vector bundles over Γ_an,r are free; closed submodules and closed ideals

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/vector-bundles-on-half-open-intervals-free` · theorem

For I bounded away from r_0 and S a collection of closed subintervals of I closed under nonempty finite intersections and such that every closed subinterval of I has a finite cover by members of S, an S-vector bundle over Γ_I is a family of finite free Γ_J-modules M_J (J ∈ S) with compatible isomorphisms M_{J_1} ⊗ Γ_{J_2} ≅ M_{J_2} for J_2 ⊆ J_1. The category does not depend on S (Kiehl-Tate type gluing). For r ∈ (0, r_0) the functor from finite free Γ_an,r-modules to vector bundles over Γ_an,r = Γ_{(0,r]} is an equivalence. Consequently every closed submodule of a finite free Γ_an,r-module is free and every closed ideal of Γ_an,r is principal. For ℓ = k((t)): every finite free ∇-module or vector bundle on a half-open annulus |π|^r ≤ |t| < 1 over a discretely valued K is given by a free module over the ring of functions (compare overview Theorem 3.4.3, stated there for spherically complete K).

**Hypotheses.**

- Enough r_0-units; O is complete discretely valued.
- Use the stated admissible interval-cover condition; merely covering the underlying set is insufficient.

**Prerequisites.** [Approximation of invertible matrices and factorisation over overlapping intervals](#target-rd-0-matrix-approximation-and-factorization) (`RD.0/matrix-approximation-and-factorization`), [Γ_r and Γ_I for closed I are principal ideal domains (Lazard)](#target-rd-0-closed-interval-analytic-ring-pid) (`RD.0/closed-interval-analytic-ring-pid`), [Numerical membership criterion, intersections and Mayer-Vietoris splitting for Γ_I](#target-rd-0-analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections) (`RD.0/analytic-ring-membership-and-intersections`).

**Sources.**

- [S2](#source-2), Theorem 2.8.4, p. 26. The statement.
- [S2](#source-2), Corollary 2.8.5, p. 27. The corollary.
- [S8](#source-8), Theorem 3.4.3, p. 14. The annulus form over spherically complete K (discretely valued fields are spherically complete).

**Construction or proof.**

1. Gluing (Lemma 2.8.2): for J ⊆ J_1 ∪ J_2 with J_1 ∩ J_2 ≠ ∅, first use Lemma 2.7.1 to choose U_0 over Γ_r[π^{-1}] with AU_0 close to the identity on the overlap; factor AU_0 = UV by Lemma 2.7.2, and absorb U_0^{-1} into the second factor and use Γ_{J_1} ∩ Γ_{J_2} = Γ_{J_1∪J_2}.
2. Theorem 2.8.4: choose closed J_1 ⊆ J_2 ⊆ ⋯ exhausting (0, r]; inductively change bases by U_i over Γ_r (approximation lemma) and by (I_n + V_i)^{-1} (truncation lemma) so that w_s(W_i − I_n) > s/r_i − 1 → ∞; the product W_1W_2⋯ converges in GL_n(Γ_an,r) and gives a global basis.
3. Corollary 2.8.5: a closed submodule gives a sub-vector bundle.

**Checks.**

- Rank-one case: a line bundle on the half-open annulus over discretely valued K is trivial (Lazard).

<a id="target-rd-0-finite-coefficient-extension-interface"></a>

### Finite coefficient extension of Laurent and Robba rings

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/finite-coefficient-extension-interface` · construction

Let L/K be a finite isometric extension of complete nonarchimedean fields. For every annulus interval I, the coefficient map A_K(I)⊗_K L→A_L(I) is a K-algebra isomorphism and a homeomorphism for the finite-dimensional tensor topology. A fixed K-basis e_1,…,e_d of L gives the inverse by taking the d coefficient-coordinate series. It also gives R_K⊗_K L≅R_L for the LF topologies and E_K⊗_K L≅E_L for the bounded-coefficient Amice norm topologies. No completed tensor is needed for finite L/K. Integral coefficient lattices are compared by uniform bounds; do not assert O_{E_L}=O_{E_K}⊗_{O_K}O_L without a separate integral-basis theorem.

**Hypotheses.**

- L/K is finite, with its given norm extending the norm of K; this is coefficient extension, not the parent finite separable residue-field extension Γ_L/Γ.
- No separability assumption is needed for this coefficient-coordinate argument; it applies in equal characteristic.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Laurent Fréchet charts and the Robba inductive limit](#target-rd-0-laurent-topology-interface) (`RD.0/laurent-topology-interface`), `mathlib:Module.Basis.equivFunL`, [Laurent, Robba and Amice coefficient carriers](#target-rd-0-laurent-robba-amice-carriers) (`RD.0/laurent-robba-amice-carriers`).

**Sources.**

- [S38](#source-38), Proof of Lemma 2.2.12, p.455, and Remark 2.3.8, p.459. Uniform coordinate bounds over a complete field and annular coefficient convergence; the coefficient-extension assertion here is the finite-coordinate consequence, not the residue-field extension of Proposition 2.4.10, p.461.
- [S43](#source-43), §2, pp.50–53. Radius norms on Laurent coefficients to which the coordinate bounds apply.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- RD.1 finite-coefficient base change: Transport Laurent convergence and Frobenius/differential matrices to a finite coefficient extension without constructing a second analytic carrier.
- Compact Laurent preparation and divisor evaluations: Evaluate polynomial roots after finite coefficient extension and use coordinate bounds to descend analytic factorisation statements.

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LaurentChart.coefficientExtension` |  | The coefficient algebra equivalence A_K(I)⊗_K L≃ₐ[K]A_L(I), with inverse given by the finite K-basis coordinates. |
| `LaurentChart.coefficientExtension_homeomorph` |  | The equivalence and its inverse are continuous for the finite-coordinate topology; it commutes with restriction of radius intervals. |
| `RobbaRing.coefficientExtension` |  | The finite-coefficient equivalence R_K⊗_K L≃ₐ[K]R_L is a homeomorphism for the final seminorm topologies, since finitely many coordinate series share an inner radius. |
| `AmiceRing.coefficientExtension` |  | The equivalence E_K⊗_K L≃ₐ[K]E_L is a homeomorphism for the bounded-coefficient norms. Its inverse coordinates have uniform bounds; this is not a claim that every basis is orthogonal. |

**Unit tests.**

- `coefficientExtension_identity` (compatibility): For L=K and the basis 1, every comparison is the identity coefficient map.
- `coefficientExtension_coordinates` (computation): For a quadratic L/K with basis 1,α, f=Σ_n(a_n+b_nα)t^n maps back to f_a⊗1+f_b⊗α; both coordinate series converge on the same I.
- `coefficientExtension_inseparable` (compatibility): For K=F_p((z)), L=K(z^{1/p}), the finite p coordinates still reconstruct all Laurent series; separability must not be added.
- `coefficientExtension_basis_bounds` (non-example): Uniform two-sided coordinate bounds do not assert exact orthogonality: for a quadratic extension of Q_p choose α∉Q_p with 0<|pα|<1. The basis 1,1+pα has two vectors of norm 1 whose difference has norm |pα|<1. Using the maximum of their unweighted coordinate norms as an exact norm is wrong.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Read the finite-basis coordinate equivalence in Mathlib at the pin. Its coordinates and inverse have uniform norm bounds independent of the Laurent index.
2. Apply those bounds to |a_n|ρ^n at every radius, and to boundedness and the negative-tail limit for E. Reconstruct the inverse finite sum Σ_j e_j f_j and verify multiplication coefficientwise using convergent convolution.
3. Apply the same uniform bounds on every compact window. For the Robba union, finitely many coordinate series share a common inner radius; the final linear topology proves continuity in both directions.

**Checks.**

- L=K is the identity comparison.
- The degree-d coordinate decomposition holds with an arbitrary basis, without demanding exact orthogonality.
- For L=K(z^{1/p}) over K=F_p((z)), coefficient extension is still an isomorphism despite inseparability.

<a id="target-rd-0-compact-laurent-preparation"></a>

### Compact Laurent preparation over arbitrary complete coefficients

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/compact-laurent-preparation` · theorem

For a complete nontrivially nonarchimedean K and a nonempty compact positive-radius annulus J, every nonzero f∈A_K(J) factors as f=P u, where P∈K[T] is the monic polynomial whose roots, with multiplicity, are exactly the zeros of f on that annulus and u is a unit in A_K(J). A power of T is absorbed in u on an annulus. On a compact disc containing zero, P also includes the zero at the centre, which cannot be absorbed in a unit. Thus A_K(J) is a principal ideal domain. Newton break radii, finite polynomial factors and invertibility are characterised on J. These statements hold in equal characteristic and without spherical completeness.

**Hypotheses.**

- Use the parent Laurent coefficients and laurent-topology-interface, not a second analytic carrier.
- Zeros can be expressed through irreducible polynomial factors and finite extension evaluation; in characteristic p separability is not assumed.
- Compact intervals may be singletons and need not be aligned with the value group.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Laurent Fréchet charts and the Robba inductive limit](#target-rd-0-laurent-topology-interface) (`RD.0/laurent-topology-interface`), [Finite coefficient extension of Laurent and Robba rings](#target-rd-0-finite-coefficient-extension-interface) (`RD.0/finite-coefficient-extension-interface`), `mathlib:IsBezout`.

**Sources.**

- [S43](#source-43), Propositions 2–4 and corollaries, §3, pp.53–56. Newton polynomial/unit factorisation and compact division/PID theory over a complete field.
- [S42](#source-42), Proposition 3.2.3, p.11. Rings of functions on closed aligned annuli are principal ideal domains, every ideal being generated by a polynomial; the overview deduces this from Lazard Proposition 4. The target drops the alignment condition, as Lazard does.
- [S44](#source-44), Théorème 2.30 and Remarque 2.31(ii), p.24. Arbitrary complete coefficient fields suffice on compact intervals.

**Construction or proof.**

1. At a radius, identify the finite block between smallest and largest dominant Laurent indices. Iterative ultrametric division factors the corresponding polynomial and a unit; completeness controls the successive corrections (Lazard Propositions 2–3).
2. On a compact window there are finitely many Newton breaks. Assemble their relatively prime polynomial factors; divide out the finite zero divisor and use the dominant-term inverse criterion for the remaining unit. For a disc include the centre order separately.
3. Lazard Proposition 4’s division/gcd argument gives principal ideals; factorisation also identifies a compact ideal generator with its finite divisor. The generic coefficient result is a new extension of the parent Γ-interval theorem, whose coefficient O is discretely valued.

**Checks.**

- On an annulus t is a unit; on a disc containing zero it has a simple zero.
- For K=F_p((z)) and J containing the radius of z^{1/p}, T^p−z is one irreducible factor; do not replace it by p distinct geometric points.
- No spherical-completeness hypothesis appears in this compact target.

<a id="target-rd-0-analytic-effective-divisors"></a>

### Effective analytic divisors over the coefficient field

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/analytic-effective-divisors` · definition

Fix a connected nonempty annulus or disc domain U and its Laurent chart A_K(U). Its closed analytic points are the monic irreducible polynomials P over K whose roots have a radius in U, with P=T included precisely when the centre belongs to U. Define an effective divisor D as a function from these points to N with locally finite support: on every compact subdomain J⊆U, only finitely many P have D(P)>0. The finite degree-weighted sum on J records geometric multiplicity. For nonzero f, div(f)(P) is the largest m for which P^m divides f near this point; compact preparation makes it well-defined and locally finite. Zero has no effective finite-multiplicity divisor. In characteristic zero this agrees with G_K-invariant locally finite geometric zero divisors, with degree multiplicities; in characteristic p use the irreducible-point form to retain inseparable multiplicities.

**Hypotheses.**

- K is complete, nontrivially nonarchimedean, of either characteristic.
- Every irreducible P has a single root radius, by the unique extended absolute value on a finite extension.
- Polynomial multiplicity at a closed point is distinguished from geometric multiplicity after inseparable extension.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`

**Prerequisites.** [Compact Laurent preparation over arbitrary complete coefficients](#target-rd-0-compact-laurent-preparation) (`RD.0/compact-laurent-preparation`), [Finite coefficient extension of Laurent and Robba rings](#target-rd-0-finite-coefficient-extension-interface) (`RD.0/finite-coefficient-extension-interface`).

**Sources.**

- [S43](#source-43), §4, (4.2)–(4.8), pp.57–58; remarks after Proposition 4 bis, p.56. On the open disc: divisors as locally finite families of normalised polynomial factors over K, the divisor of a function, the divisibility criterion (4.7) and the unit criterion (4.8). After Proposition 4 bis, whose proof Lazard only outlines, he reduces zeros on an annulus to zeros on discs; the annulus case here applies the same definition window by window.
- [S44](#source-44), Préface §2.5.1 and Théorème 2.30(ii), p.24. Characteristic-zero Galois-invariant locally finite zero divisors; zero ideal is handled separately here.

**Uses and API requirements.**

- Lazard Proposition 10: Describe closed ideals by their common divisors.
- Lazard Theorem 2 and Colmez Théorème 2.30: Prescribed zeros and principality on noncompact domains.

**API.**

| Declaration | Role | Statement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AnalyticDivisor.zero` |  | The everywhere-zero multiplicity function is a locally finite effective divisor. |
| `AnalyticDivisor.add` |  | Addition adds multiplicities and preserves local finiteness. |
| `AnalyticDivisor.inf` |  | Pointwise minimum is an effective divisor and computes a common zero divisor. |
| `AnalyticDivisor.restrict` |  | Restrict D to a subdomain by retaining its closed points; restrictions compose. |
| `AnalyticDivisor.ofNonzero` |  | div(f) is defined for f≠0 and has the compact factor orders as multiplicities. |
| `AnalyticDivisor.mul` |  | For f,g≠0, div(fg)=div(f)+div(g); div(f)=0 iff f is a unit on U. |
| `AnalyticDivisor.geometric_comparison` |  | In characteristic zero, the irreducible-point divisor corresponds to the Galois-invariant geometric divisor on the algebraic closure. |

**Unit tests.**

- `divisor_unit` (computation): div(1)=0. On an annulus div(t)=0; on a disc containing zero div(t) has multiplicity 1 at T.
- `divisor_inseparable` (compatibility): For K=F_p((z)), P=T^p−z contributes one closed-point multiplicity and geometric multiplicity p at its single root; p distinct points is wrong.
- `divisor_accumulation_interior` (non-example): An infinite list of distinct zeros accumulating at an interior radius violates local finiteness, even if each individual point has multiplicity 1.
- `divisor_zero_function` (non-example): No finite effective divisor is assigned to the identically zero function; adding such a divisor destroys the ideal correspondence.

**Construction or proof.**

1. Use existing polynomial irreducibility and the unique extension of the norm, rather than importing a new space of geometric points.
2. Compact preparation identifies the local factor order and proves consistency under restricting compact windows. A compact exhaustion gives the global divisor and local finiteness.
3. Define addition and pointwise minimum; restrict by retaining points in the smaller domain. Verify the geometric comparison over characteristic-zero coefficients by finite Galois orbits.

**Checks.**

- The zero function is excluded from div; the zero divisor is allowed.

<a id="target-rd-0-analytic-divisor-majorant"></a>

### A nonzero function dominating a locally finite divisor

`PadicDifferentialEquationsAndRigidCohomology:RD.0/analytic-divisor-majorant` · theorem

For any effective locally finite D on an annulus or disc U over a complete nonarchimedean K, there exists nonzero f∈A_K(U) with D≤div(f). Extra zeros are allowed. This statement needs no spherical completeness and does not imply that D itself is a principal divisor.

**Hypotheses.**

- The domain and the divisor are those of analytic-effective-divisors.

**Intended library interface.** `TauCeti/RigidCohomology/Foundations`, `TauCeti.RigidCohomology`
