F_0 and F_1 are the kernel and cokernel of the vertical connection on E itself, Proposition 3.2.5 is applied to E with R^0 f_*E = F_0 = 0, and the conclusion drawn is '(b) holds on X' for E.

**E63 — [S5](#source-5), §6.6 (b), functional equation, p. 52.** P_{2n−i}(t) = c·t^{b_i}·P_i(q^{−n}t^{−1}) with b_i = deg P_i and c = (−1)^{b_i} q^{n b_i}/det(F | H^i). Poincaré duality pairs eigenvalue α on H^i with q^n/α on H^{2n−i}. For P^1 (n = 1): P_0 = 1 − t, P_2 = 1 − qt, while c·t^j·P_0(1/t) = c(t^j − t^{j−1}) is never 1 − qt.

**E64 — [S5](#source-5), §6.6, proof of (a), p. 52.** With this choice P_i ∈ 1 + tK[t]; integrality of each P_i is not a consequence of these two inputs. The existence statement (a) follows from rationality (Z ∈ K(t) ∩ Q[[t]] = Q(t)) and Fatou's lemma; for smooth proper X the individual P_i are integral by (c) and weight separation (RD.7/weil-factors-rational-and-integral). The trace formula and finiteness only give an identity in K[[t]] for the alternating product; they say nothing about the coefficients of an individual factor.

**E65 — [S6](#source-6), §3, basis of the + eigenspace, p. 4.** i = 0, …, 2g: the + eigenspace is H^1 of A^1 minus the 2g + 1 roots of Q, of dimension 2g + 1. H^1(C')^+ ≅ H^1(A^1 − {roots of Q}) has dimension 2g + 1 (residues at the 2g + 1 roots are independent); x^{2g} dx/Q(x) has nonzero residue at ∞ and is not in the span of the others.

**E66 — [S6](#source-6), §3, reduction to a_1, …, a_g, p. 6.** a_{2g−i} = q^{g−i} a_i (from α_j α_{g+j} = q). PARI/GP: for y^2 = x^5 + x + 3 over F_7 the Frobenius polynomial is x^4 + 3x^3 + 7x^2 + 21x + 49, so a_1 = 3 ≠ 21 = a_3 = 7·a_1.

**E67 — [S6](#source-6), Lemma 3, p. 5.** Corrected in the errata: for F_j(x) y^e dx the multiplier is p^m with m = ⌊log_p((2g + 1)(e + 2) − 2)⌋ (as quoted by Harvey, arXiv math/0610973v2 §3). Harvey §3 points out the error in the original Lemma 3, cites its corrected statement in Kedlaya’s errata and directs the reader to Edixhoven Lemma 4.3.5 for a proof.

**E218 — [S27](#source-27), Proposition 11.2.24, statement, p. 378, author copy courbe.pdf (16 avril 2017); page image checked.** Only a filtration descends (Kedlaya [45] Prop. 5.11): every (V, ϕ) ∈ ϕ-Mod_{E†} has a unique filtration by saturated sub-ϕ-modules with isoclinic graded pieces of strictly decreasing Dieudonné–Manin slopes (each a direct sum of E†(λ) when F is algebraically closed). The completion functor is essentially surjective and an equivalence on isoclinic objects, but not fully faithful, and ϕ-modules over E† are not in general direct sums of E†(λ). Choose c of absolute value greater than one. In the rank-two example F(e₁)=e₁+[c]e₂ and F(e₂)=πe₂, the completed fixed vector uses y=Σ_(k≥0)π^k[c^(q^k)]. This solves y−πF(y)=[c] in the π-adic completion but fails every positive-radius overconvergence bound. Thus completion adds a fixed vector, and an integral endomorphism of determinant π cannot satisfy the claimed invariant descent. The matrix equation for a fixed vector is X=A F(X); applying the source’s argument requires the integral inverse of A.

**E219 — [S27](#source-27), Lemme 11.2.25, statement and proof (equation (7)), p. 379, author copy courbe.pdf (16 avril 2017); page image checked.** Assume ϕ bijective on Λ (matrix A ∈ GL_n(O_{E†})). Then a fixed vector satisfies X = Aϕ(X), i.e. ϕ(X) = A^{−1}X, and the printed argument applies to A^{−1} (after rescaling the basis so that A^{−1} mod π ∈ M_n(O_F)). Choose c of absolute value greater than one. In the rank-two example F(e₁)=e₁+[c]e₂ and F(e₂)=πe₂, the completed fixed vector uses y=Σ_(k≥0)π^k[c^(q^k)]. This solves y−πF(y)=[c] in the π-adic completion but fails every positive-radius overconvergence bound. Thus completion adds a fixed vector, and an integral endomorphism of determinant π cannot satisfy the claimed invariant descent. The matrix equation for a fixed vector is X=A F(X); applying the source’s argument requires the integral inverse of A.

**E68 — [S32](#source-32), §2.1.5, p. 10, arXiv:1910.13391 (SHA-256 recorded in sources).** For that connection and map direction, use exp(π(t^p−t)); equivalently the printed exponential gives the reverse map. The trace-character normalization must invert at the same time. A horizontal multiplier h must satisfy dh/h=π(pt^(p−1)−1)dt. Differentiating the printed multiplier gives its negative. This is the same sign obstruction independently recorded for Kedlaya in E13.

**E69 — [S32](#source-32), §2.1.5, p. 10, arXiv:1910.13391 (SHA-256 recorded in sources).** For the q-power pullback that admits this multiplier, the connection coefficient is aq. A p-power pullback would instead require t^((p−1)a) together with its coefficient Frobenius. The multiplier satisfies dh/h=(q−1)a dt/t. Horizontality for ∇=d−a dt/t therefore requires the pulled-back coefficient qa, and the stated integrality condition (q−1)a∈Z also fixes that q convention.

**E70 — [S2](#source-2), Corollary 2.5.7, proof, p.19, arXiv v4.** Take the semiunit presentation over I, then use Lemma2.5.4 to extend its convergence to J. At this point only x∈Γ_I is known; using Γ_J is circular.

**E71 — [S2](#source-2), Definition 2.8.1 and Lemma 2.8.2, pp.26–27, arXiv v4.** Require every compact subinterval to admit a finite covering by members, including suitable interval neighbourhoods for the gluing argument. The family of all singleton intervals permits unrelated modules at each radius, with no transition compatibility between distinct radii; arbitrary such data cannot come from one finite-free Γ_I-module.

**E72 — [S2](#source-2), Lemma 2.9.1, proof, p.28, arXiv v4.** It is a unit on [s,r]; divisibility of f by the resulting g on [s′,r] follows by the separate slope argument. A unit on [s′,r] cannot remove a zero or slope lying in [s′,s).

**E73 — [S2](#source-2), Remark 4.5.2, p.49, arXiv v4.** Use eigenvectors with their individual eigenvalues; fixed vectors supply a basis only in slope zero. A positive-slope rank-one standard module has no nonzero Frobenius-fixed vectors, although it has a standard eigenbasis.

**E74 — [S2](#source-2), Lemma 4.5.5, statement and proof, pp.49–50, arXiv v4.** The constant-term extraction in the proof constructs some descending eigenbasis; arbitrary eigenbases need not descend. For M=O[π⁻¹](−1)⊕O[π⁻¹](0), choose a nonconstant analytic x with σ(x)=πx (as in Remark3.3.6). Then e₁,e₂+xe₁ is an eigenbasis over R but its second vector is not constant. The proof’s constant-term projection produces a different basis.

**E75 — [S2](#source-2), Proposition 5.1.2, p.54, arXiv v4.** The isomorphism is σ*N→N for the chosen integral lattice N. F:σ*M→M is already invertible by the definition of a σ-module; the added unit-root conclusion concerns its integral lattice.

**E76 — [S2](#source-2), Proposition 5.5.4, p.60, arXiv v4.** Require w_r(AD⁻¹−I)>0 as well as w(AD⁻¹−I)>0. The expression is not a proposition without a comparison; the subsequent matrix-lifting argument uses positivity at both valuations.

**E77 — [S8](#source-8), Lemma 4.2.7, p.19, arXiv v2.** Use Hom_G(Res_G^H V,W)≅Hom_H(V,Ind_G^H W), for coinduction identified with induction for finite groups. Restriction maps H-representations to G-representations; the printed expression has its domain categories reversed.

**E78 — [S8](#source-8), Remark 4.4.2, p.21, arXiv v2.** Use the full long exact cohomology sequences, the dual connecting arrows and their residue-pairing compatibility. An extension of trivial lines with nonzero logarithmic connection has a nonzero connecting map H⁰(quotient)→H¹(submodule), so the claimed terminal surjectivity fails.

**E79 — [S8](#source-8), Proposition 5.2.3, proof, pp.29–30, arXiv v2.** Use parallel transport from the fibre at the centre, or the evaluated horizontal projection with the matching sign and pullback convention. For a rank-one connection D(e)=ae with a≠0, the unevaluated positive series is exp(a(t−z))e and its covariant derivative is 2a times itself.

**E80 — [S1](#source-1), Lemma 2.3, p.14, arXiv v4.** Require n≥2 for the SL_n assertion; in dimension one use GL₁ or require the entry to be one. Over Q₂ the one-entry row (2) is unimodular, but SL₁ consists only of the identity and cannot have first row (2).

**E81 — [S1](#source-1), Lemma 2.6, p.15, arXiv v4.** Add I≠0. The zero ideal is stable under every action, but contains no nonzero fixed generator of the asserted type.

**E82 — [S16](#source-16), Proposition 3.3, proof, block matrix equation, p.7, arXiv v4.** For change of basis [[I,X],[0,I]], solve B+AX^σ−XD=0, hence −X+AX^σD⁻¹=−BD⁻¹. With A=2,D=3,B=5 and σ=id, the equation has X=5; the printed right-hand side does not.

**E83 — [S16](#source-16), Proposition 3.3, proof, change of basis z_i=y_i−ΣU_ijv_j, p.8, arXiv v4.** With F(y)=μy+Vv and F(v)=λv, require μU−λσ(U)=−V. Substituting y−Uv into F gives the stated coefficient equation directly; the printed relation does not cancel the off-diagonal term.

**E84 — [S16](#source-16), Lemmas 6.2–6.3 and Propositions 6.4–6.6, pp.13–15, arXiv v4.** Supply the rank-one valued-field version of that lemma and the projective-module/free-resolution algebra before using the broader target. The integral target here is restricted to a DVR. Lemma6.2 explicitly assumes a discrete valuation while Proposition6.4 removes it. The inherited author-erratum attribution was not independently accessible; this finding is restricted to the public proof.

**E85 — [S4](#source-4), Definition 2.1.9, p.10, arXiv v6.** A⟨f⁻¹⟩ represents maps for which the chosen inverse of f has norm at most one; allow the zero algebra and a noninjective map from A. For f=π with |π|<1, A already contains π⁻¹ algebraically, but A⟨π⁻¹⟩=0 because 1−πT is invertible in the Tate algebra.

**E86 — [S4](#source-4), Definition 2.2.2, p.11, arXiv v6.** Complete in the affinoid norm, or use a ring of definition and its uniformiser-adic topology before inverting the uniformiser. The K-algebra contains the topologically nilpotent unit π. The ideal it generates is the whole algebra, whose ideal-adic completion is zero.

**E87 — [S4](#source-4), Remark 2.3.6, p.13, arXiv v6.** Its norm there is ρ>1; scalar constants at the unit boundary distinguish the affinoid and fringe topologies by a different example, not this assertion. Gauss norms give ‖x₁^m‖_ρ=ρ^m, which grows rather than tends to zero. The earlier corollary in the same section also contradicts the printed example.

**E88 — [S4](#source-4), Remark 3.2.4, p.21, arXiv v6.** Use the finite-flat relative Frobenius after coefficient extension; absolute Frobenius is finite only with the relevant F-finiteness hypothesis. For a residue field with an infinite p-basis, k/k^p is infinite and absolute Frobenius is not finite even on Spec k.

**E89 — [S4](#source-4), Lemma 5.2.7, p.32, arXiv v6.** Permit a≥0. Use the Vandermonde expansion of binom(m+l+x,l) and bounds on coefficients of binom(x,j), including negative m. For e=1 the upper bound is zero, so no positive a can satisfy it. For m=−1,l=1 the product is x and the printed division by m+1 is undefined.

**E90 — [S4](#source-4), Lemma 6.2.6, p.38, arXiv v6.** Use c(d(r)+1), accounting for a finite basis of the constant-field extension. A nontrivial constant-field element has pole degree zero but may require positive degree in the given k-algebra generators.

**E91 — [S4](#source-4), Lemma 6.2.8, p.38, arXiv v6.** Require both a and b nonzero. For A=K⟨t⟩† and a=0, the source is zero while the principal-parts target at infinity is infinite-dimensional, so the map is not a near-isomorphism.

**E92 — [S4](#source-4), Proposition 7.2.1, p.45, arXiv v6.** Keep flat base change. To remove flatness prove the additional Frobenius constraints make the constant-matrix kernel and cokernel commute with arbitrary base change. Cohomology is ker N and coker N of the constant nilpotent matrix. Nonflat tensor products need not preserve its kernel; the displayed filtration alone does not settle this. This is a proof gap, not a counterexample to the F-module theorem.

**E93 — [S4](#source-4), §8.5, chain pairing after Lemma 8.5.2, p.59, arXiv v6.** For v of degree i use [v,∇w]=(−1)^(i+1)[∇v,w] under the residue convention. In two variables take v=t₁dt₂ and w=1/(t₁t₂). Both residues are one; degree-one integration by parts requires a plus sign.

**E94 — [S5](#source-5), §1.5, elliptic slopes and weights discussion, p.7, arXiv v3.** For the Kronecker argument establish that quotient is an algebraic unit at every finite place and all its complex conjugates have absolute value one. The Weil25 polynomial T⁴−4T³+35T²−100T+625 has p=5 slopes 0,1,1,2. The middle pair is balanced at that place without providing a global-unit criterion.

**E95 — [S5](#source-5), §6.1, realisation by E⊕E∨(−w), p.40, arXiv v3.** Use this formula for integer w. For real w, enlarge coefficients and tensor the dual with a constant line having complex Frobenius q^w, after verifying the scalar-normalisation existence. Tate twists in the coefficient category are indexed by integers. They cannot be applied directly to a nonintegral real weight. Purity of E is also necessary for the realisation argument.

**E96 — [S5](#source-5), Proposition 6.3.1(i), p.45, arXiv v3.** Require finite dominant (hence surjective) pullback for the equivalence. The finite map from the empty scheme detects no weights at all; a non-dominant finite fibre likewise cannot determine a varying object on the whole base.

**E97 — [S5](#source-5), Proposition 6.4.4, proof, pp.47–48, arXiv v3.** Use a justified tensor-invariant or weight-monodromy argument; this false inclusion is not a proof of the theorem. Let Ne₂=e₁ and Ne₁=0 in a size-two Jordan block. Then e₁ is horizontal but N(e₁⊗e₂)=e₁⊗e₁≠0.

**E98 — [S5](#source-5), Lemma 6.7.2, proof, p.53, arXiv v3.** The constant coefficient has nonzero H¹_c in general. A proper-curve crystalline lattice plus localisation can supply the nonnegative-slope input, but must be planned and proved. For G_m, H¹_c(K)=K is nonzero and has slope zero. The lemma’s conclusion survives this example; its stated vanishing proof does not.

**E101 — [S38](#source-38), Example 2.2.18, journal p.456; arXiv v4 p.10.** Require finite coefficient p-rank for this particular Laurent monomial basis, or independently assume an actual valuation p-basis of the complete residue field. For k=F_p(s_1,s_2,…) with independent indeterminates, Σ_{n≥1}s_n t^{pn} has infinitely many nonzero coordinates in distinct constant p-monomials over k^p((t^p)). A finite monomial sum cannot represent it. This invalidates this proposed basis, not the existence of any other valuation p-basis.

**E102 — [S38](#source-38), Proof of Proposition 2.2.21(c), journal p.457; arXiv v4 p.11.** Use y_i+c_i y_1. Both inspected versions correctly say that the x_i are dependent; no correction of that wording is needed. Make the DVR relation primitive before choosing a unit coefficient to express x_1. Bilinearity gives x_1⊗y_1=Σ x_i⊗c_i y_1. Even over Z, taking y_1=2 shows the omitted factor changes the tensor. The corrected rewrite decreases its length.

**E103 — [S44](#source-44), Théorème 2.30(ii), printed p.24, April 2017 author copy only.** Restrict the finite effective-divisor bijection to nonzero closed ideals and treat the zero ideal separately. Zero is a closed ideal whose generator is the zero function. Its orders are infinite at every point, so it has no locally finite effective divisor with natural-number multiplicities.

**E104 — [S45](#source-45), Proof of Proposition 3.6, printed p.43, author manuscript.** The sum is αTr(c)=α. Keep the scalar α in the subtraction used to estimate Tr(cα)−α. α is fixed as an external factor in this sum, so factoring it out gives αΣ_σ σ(c). The subsequent conjugate-difference estimate uses this corrected equality.

**E105 — [S44](#source-44), Préface §2.5.1, printed p.24, April 2017 author copy only.** Use the already-defined v_J=inf_{r∈J}v_r, equivalently the compact endpoint Gauss maximum after converting to norms. Any pointwise reformulation needs an infimum with a sufficient set of valued extension points, not a sum. For the constant f=p on a nonempty annulus, v_J(f)=1, whereas summing the value 1 over its infinitely many analytic points cannot give 1.

**E106 — [S44](#source-44), Préface §2.5.1, printed p.24, April 2017 author copy only.** For a disc containing the centre complete polynomials (nonnegative powers); for positive-radius annuli use Laurent polynomials. T^{-1} has a pole at the centre and its Gauss value at +∞ is not finite. It cannot be an analytic element or a member of a finite-norm polynomial starting space for that disc.

**E301 — [S48](#source-48), KX arXiv v4 Lemma 2.3.2 proof, p. 23.** Use Lemma 2.3.1. Lemma 2.3.1 is the preceding finite-locally-free intersection statement needed on End(M).

**E302 — [S48](#source-48), KX arXiv v4 Theorem 2.6.1 proof, pp. 32–33.** Use Theorem 2.5.1 for the boundary annulus. A neighbourhood of the outer Robba boundary excludes t=0; Theorem 2.5.1 is precisely the affine-gap annular statement.

**E303 — [S28](#source-28), D’Addezio arXiv v4 Theorem 4.2.6(i), p. 14.** Use S_(m+1−i)/S_(m−i), 1≤i≤m. At i=m the printed expression reaches a negative index; the last reverse grade is the lowest ascending grade S₁/S₀.

**E304 — [S52](#source-52), Hartl–Pink published §10.17, p. 712.** The left side must be log|w−w_i|. The preceding root-lifting estimate is logarithmic; absolute values are nonnegative.

**E305 — [S52](#source-52), Hartl–Pink published §10.16, p. 712.** Use log|w|=−ρ≤−cn. Lemma 10.12 chooses ρ≥cn, and §10.3 requires log|w|≤−cn. The printed inequality −ρ≤cn is true but too weak to feed §10.3; the construction gives −ρ≤−cn.

**E306 — [S14](#source-14), Monodromy published Lemma 4.12 proof, p. 150.** Use U_h(t). h(t) is the uniform lower valuation bound; f depends on two additional indices and cannot label that module.

**E307 — [S14](#source-14), Monodromy published Lemma 4.12 proof, p. 150, bilateral series estimate.** Use l v_p(π)+s q^(−l)t throughout. The residue contribution to w_s is multiplied by the same radius s as on its left side.

**E308 — [S14](#source-14), Monodromy published Proposition 5.11 proof, p. 165.** It is the highest slope line in the d-th exterior power. M₁ was selected as the highest-slope rank-d block; summing its d slopes maximises the exterior-power slope.

**E309 — [S14](#source-14), Monodromy published Proposition 5.11 proof, p. 165, coefficient induction base.** The coordinates reduce to δᵢ₁; normalise wᵢ≡vᵢ modulo π. v₁ has coordinate one in the first vector and zero in the other vectors in a nearby basis. The first coordinate is a unit, and the displayed bound still follows.

**E310 — [S14](#source-14), Monodromy published Lemma 4.12 proof, definition of b₂ and the telescoping step, p. 151.** Read a sum from j=1 to N with N<0 as minus the sum from j=N+1 to 0 (oriented summation). With this convention b₂−πσⁿ(b₂)=r(z)−A holds for every pair in T. i+l−s(i,l) can be negative. Take q=2, n=1 and one coefficient u₀ with v₀(u₀)=−1, so f(0,l,m)=−2^(−l)+m4^(−l). The corners of h are t=(2/3)2^l, with h(t)=−2^(−l)/3. At t=(2/3)2^(−5) the pair (0,−5) lies in S, so s=0 and i+l−s=−5; an empty sum would break the telescoping for this pair. With T_j=π^(i+l−j)σ^(−nj)(u_iσ^(−l)(z)) one has πσⁿ(T_j)=T_(j−1), and the oriented sum S of T_1,…,T_N satisfies S−πσⁿ(S)=T_N−T_0 for every integer N.

**E311 — [S48](#source-48), KX arXiv v4 Theorem 2.6.1 proof, first sentence, p. 33.** The index is i: for i=1,…,d the function d!F_i(M,r) is continuous, convex and piecewise affine with integer slopes. Only i occurs in the rest of the sentence and the proof; l plays no role.

**E-RD2-1 — [S57](#source-57), Theorem 19.4.1 and Corollary 19.4.2, p. 321 (first edition, author's PDF).** The intrinsic radius is meant: IR(D†(V) ⊗ F_ρ) = ρ^b, i.e. R(D†(V) ⊗ F_ρ) = ρ^{b+1}, with b the highest upper break of V restricted to inertia (Serre's numbering), b ∈ Q_{≥0}, b = 0 when V is tamely ramified; the restriction i ≥ 1 must be dropped because highest breaks in (0, 1) occur. Likewise the subsidiary radii in Corollary 19.4.2 are intrinsic. Dwork's rank-one module M_f with f = t^{−1} (Example 17.1.4, = D†(V) for the Artin-Schreier character of break 1 by Example 19.2.6) has horizontal section exp(π_0(t^{−1} − t_ρ^{−1})) (with the connection sign of E-RD2-12; the radius does not depend on the sign) converging exactly on |t − t_ρ| < ρ^2, so R = ρ^2 while the printed formula gives ρ^1; the book's own Theorem 12.6.4 and Definition 9.4.4 (R = ρ for the trivial module) and Kedlaya's overview (Definition 5.4.1, Theorem 5.4.10) give R = ρ^{β+1}. Inducing the break-1 Artin-Schreier character from k((t^{1/2})) (p odd) gives a representation with highest upper break 1/2, for which no i ≥ 1 qualifies.

**E-RD2-2 — [S32](#source-32), §2.9.2, display (2.9.2.2), p. 24 (arXiv:1910.13391, page image checked).** Sol(M) is canonically the dual (Coker N)^∨ = ker(N^∨ on V^∨): a horizontal homomorphism is a constant functional λ on V with λ∘N = 0. Writing φ(v) = Σ φ_n(v) x^n, horizontality gives φ_n∘N = nφ_n, so φ_n = 0 for n ≥ 1 (N − n invertible) and φ_0 vanishes on NV; for M = U_2 the solutions form the annihilator of e_1 in V^∨. The dimensions agree, and that is all the paper's subsequent argument uses (convergence of solutions in the proof of Proposition 5.1.3).

**E-RD2-3 — [S60](#source-60), Definition 2.5.1, p. 462 (Doc. Math. 10; arXiv v4 p. 16), used in Proposition 3.3.7(c), Proposition 4.2.2, Lemmas 4.3.1-4.3.2.** The construction is invalid because the Teichmüller map is not additive; in Proposition 3.3.7(c), Proposition 4.2.2 and Lemma 4.3.2 use strong semiunit presentations (as in the Annals paper, Proposition 3.14) instead; the surjectivity in Lemma 4.3.1, which needs uniqueness, follows from Fourquaux's thesis, Corollaire 3.9.19, and is not used elsewhere. Pointed out by L. Berger and corrected by the author in the published erratum.

**E-RD2-4 — [S60](#source-60), Lemma 2.9.1, statement p. 474, proof p. 475 (Doc. Math. 10; arXiv v4 p. 28 for both).** Obtain g with (a), (b) from Lemma 2.6.7; for (c) choose s″ with no slopes of f in [s″, s), divide in Γ_[s″,r], note g is a unit in Γ_[s′,s″], and glue the two divisibilities using Corollary 2.5.7 (Γ_[s′,s″] ∩ Γ_[s″,r] = Γ_[s′,r]). Observed by R. Liu and repaired in the published erratum; this is the issue the underlying construction recorded as its E72 as new.

**E-RD2-5 — [S60](#source-60), Lemma 2.9.3, proof, p. 475 (Doc. Math. 10; arXiv v4: statement p. 28, proof p. 29).** Replace g_{i+1} − x_i by y_i ∈ Γ_r with g_{i+1} − x_i − y_i divisible by h_{i+1} in Γ_{i+1}, chosen by an argument like Lemma 2.9.2. Observed by R. Liu and repaired in the published erratum.

**E-RD2-6 — [S1](#source-1), Introduction (Section 1.1), p. 3 of arXiv:math/0110124v4 (p. 95 of the Annals version).** An element of Γcon has that property only after multiplication by a large power of the series variable (and conversely); Γcon is the ring of bounded-by-1 overconvergent series in the sense of Chapter 3. Pointed out by K. Buzzard and corrected in the erratum to Slope filtrations revisited; for example u^{−1} ∈ Γcon has |u^{−1}| = 1/|u| > 1 on every annulus ρ < |u| < 1, while u·u^{−1} = 1 is integral.

**E-RD2-7 — [S1](#source-1), Lemma 2.3, p. 14 of arXiv:math/0110124v4 (Annals version, Lemma 2.3).** R must be a Bézout domain: the proof divides by a generator d of (x_1, …, x_{n−1}), which needs d to be a nonzerodivisor. The induction forms x_i/d; in a ring with zero divisors a generator need not divide its multiples uniquely. Corrected by the author.

**E-RD2-8 — [S8](#source-8), Lemma 5.4.6, p. 33 (arXiv:math/0501361v2; page image checked).** E has highest break ≥ β (resp. ≤ β) iff f^*E has highest break ≥ nβ (resp. ≤ nβ) iff f_*E has highest break ≥ β/n (resp. ≤ β/n). Each clause compares one-sided bounds; with 'exactly nβ' the equivalence fails, e.g. E of highest break 2β has highest break ≥ β while f^*E has highest break 2nβ ≠ nβ. The proof (Lemma 5.3.1) gives the one-sided statements.

**E-RD2-9 — [S8](#source-8), Proof of Lemma 5.4.7, p. 33 (arXiv:math/0501361v2; page image checked).** That ring reduces to u^p − u = −a t^{−n} (expand (1 + πu)^p = 1 + pπu − pπu^p + higher terms and divide by pπ); take b lifting −a, or replace u by −u when p is odd. The cover is the same up to this sign, so nothing downstream changes. Coefficient comparison modulo pπ^2: π^p = −pπ and the middle binomial terms are divisible by pπ^2.

**E-RD2-10 — [S57](#source-57), Lemma 19.3.3, proof, last paragraph, pp. 319-320 (first edition, author's PDF).** For the standard lift φ(t) = t^q, (17.1.2.1) reads NA + t dA/dt = qAφ(N), that is N − qAφ(N)A^{−1} = −t(dA/dt)A^{−1}; the proof of Lemma 19.3.4 on the next page writes the relation correctly. The argument only uses which powers of t occur, so nothing changes. Rank one: the module E† v with t dv/dt = v/(q − 1) and F(v) = t·v satisfies (17.1.2.1), since NA + t dA/dt = t/(q − 1) + t = q·t/(q − 1) = qAφ(N); the printed form fails, since there N − qAφ(N)A^{−1} = −1 while t(dA/dt)A^{−1} = 1.

**E-RD2-11 — [S8](#source-8), Proof of Lemma 5.4.7, pp. 33-34 (arXiv:math/0501361v2; page images checked).** p·d(1 + πu)^i/(1 + πu)^i = i·d(1 + pπbt^{−n})/(1 + pπbt^{−n}), so the summand generated by (1 + πu)^i has ∇v = −iπnbt^{−n−1}(1 + pπbt^{−n})^{−1} v ⊗ dt, and in the rest of the proof the horizontal section is exp(−iπb(t^{−n} − t_ρ^{−n}))w. The convergence radius ρ^{n+1}, hence the break n, is unchanged because |i| = 1. (1 + πu)^p = 1 + pπbt^{−n} gives p·dlog(1 + πu) = dlog(1 + pπbt^{−n}), and dlog((1 + πu)^i) = i·dlog(1 + πu). The p − 1 nontrivial summands correspond to the p − 1 distinct nontrivial characters of Z/p, so they are pairwise non-isomorphic and cannot all equal one module.

**E-RD2-12 — [S57](#source-57), Example 17.1.4, p. 292 (first edition, author's PDF); used in Example 19.2.6, p. 317.** These two do not match: for D(v) = π(df/dt)v the compatibility (17.1.1.1) forces Φ(v) = exp(πφ(f) − πf)v; equivalently, keep Φ and take D(v) = −π(df/dt)v. With the second reading, Example 19.2.6 (D†(V) = M_f for the character sending z ↦ z + 1 to ζ_p, where 1 − ζ_p ≡ π modulo π^2) holds as printed. In rank one (17.1.1.1) reads Na + da/dt = (dφ(t)/dt)·a·φ(N); with N = π df/dt it gives dlog a = π d(φ(f)) − π df, so a = exp(π(φ(f) − f)) up to a constant, as also follows from Φ carrying the horizontal section exp(−πf)v to a multiple of itself. For Example 19.2.6 with f = t^{−1}: in E†[u]/((1 + πu)^p − 1 − pπt^{−1}) the automorphism z ↦ z + 1 (z = −ū) multiplies 1 + πu by ζ_p, so D†(V) is spanned by (1 + πu)^{−1}, whose connection form πt^{−2}(1 + pπt^{−1})^{−1} dt matches −π(df/dt) dt.

**E301 — [S62](#source-62), (2.3.2)(iii), p. 71 (IRMAR 96-03, version provisoire 1991).** Independence follows by passing to a common refinement embedded in the products P_α ×_S P′_β, using the frame-independence equivalences on each piece and the uniqueness and transitivity of the Taylor comparison isomorphisms; the argument is written out in isocrystals-glued-from-local-frames. The step is needed for the gluing construction to define a category up to canonical equivalence, on which the independence of the compactification (2.3.5) and the definition (2.3.6) rely.

**E302 — [S62](#source-62), Proof of (2.3.5), p. 73.** The locality in X is the remark after (2.2.11) (together with (2.3.3)(i)); (2.2.17) concerns two morphisms with the same restriction to Y′. (2.2.17) constructs the comparison isomorphism between pullbacks along morphisms agreeing on Y′ and says nothing about restriction to opens of X; the stack statement used here is the remark after (2.2.11).

**E303 — [S20](#source-20), (4.3), Théorème 5, p. 30.** The statement is proved in Tsuzuki, 'On base change theorem and coherence in rigid cohomology', Documenta Math. Extra Volume Kato (2003), Theorem 4.1.1, pp. 906–908, which attributes it to Berthelot. Mém. SMF 23 is a survey announcing results of the then unwritten preprint; the theorem is used by Étesse (2002, proof of Théorème 7) through this citation.

**E1 — [S71](#source-71), arXiv:1408.3329v1, Lemma 4.7 and its author footnote, p. 21; the footnote reports an omission in the 2000 publication, whose text was not independently read here.** Use the corrected author-version lemma with both hypotheses. Theorem 5.1 here already assumes a complete mixed-characteristic DVR. The author footnote explicitly restores the hypotheses to make the finiteness input available. This records a known repair to the proof assumptions, without alleging a new counterexample or independently collating the publisher text.

**E2 — [S72](#source-72), arXiv:1408.3346v1, §5.2, unnumbered alternating intersection complex following equation (2), p. 28; finding scoped to this author version.** The second sum is indexed by Θ_(2,G); later terms use successively higher intersection orders. Equation (2) identifies Gr_j with j-fold intersections. Thus the Gr_2 term is indexed by Θ_(2,G). For two transverse components the first sum has the two components and the next sum their single intersection; repeating the component sum cannot be the displayed residue exact sequence.

**E3 — [S36](#source-36), Published PDF, Remark 11.7.2 and Proposition 11.7.3, p. 210; report concerns the first version, not the corrected published theorem.** Require a split hypercover in that compactification construction, or use the separate proof for a general hypercover. Theorem 9.1.1, used here for an already supplied étale-proper frame hypercover, is unchanged. The corrected remark and Proposition 11.7.3 explicitly require splitness to construct the simplicial proper completion. The remark also explains that descent itself has another proof without splitness; the omission concerns this proof route.

**E501 — [S25](#source-25), Lemma 6, proof, p. 4, arXiv:math/0303382v3; published version not inspected.** Use δ_i = β_i α^{2l−j_i} + γ_i² ∈ Γ(L^{2l}); then δ_i/α^{2l} = f_i + (γ_i/α^l)². The two printed summands have degrees l−j_i and 2l and cannot be added as sections of the stated bundle. The corrected powers give degree 2l in both terms and preserve the differential on S because γ_i vanishes there.

**E502 — [S19](#source-19), Proposition 3.10, printed p. 726, published Numdam article; compare proof of Proposition 3.11, p. 727.** Test only bounded convex linearly compact subsets C of f(V), with the topology induced from W. The inclusion K → K², x ↦ (x,0), is strict and has strict transpose (a,b) ↦ a. The bounded linearly compact set O_K·(0,1) in W has no inverse image under f. The condition on subsets of f(V) passes this example and is the image in which the subsequent proof lifts null sequences.

**E-RD6-1 — [S92](#source-92), Section 2.1.5 (ii), p. 10, arXiv:1910.13391v2.** In the direction F^*K_a → K_a, the horizontal multiplier for ∇ = d − a dx/x is t^{−(q−1)a}; the printed multiplier t^{(q−1)a} is horizontal for the reverse direction K_a → F^*K_a (or, in the printed direction, for ∇ = d + a dx/x). The trace function χ ∘ Norm with χ(x) = x̃^{(q−1)a} belongs to the printed multiplier; in the pullback-to-module convention of this roadmap it corresponds to ∇e = a·e ⊗ dx/x (RD.6/kummer-isocrystal). For F(σ^*e) = h·e with ∇e = −a e dt/t and σ^*(dt/t) = q dt/t, horizontality gives dh/h − a dt/t = −qa dt/t, so dh/h = −(q − 1)a dt/t. The roadmap's E69 corrects the misprint p for q in the pulled-back coefficient, but its horizontality inference (dh/h = (q − 1)a dt/t for ∇ = d − a dt/t) holds only in the module-to-pullback direction, not in the pullback-to-module direction Xu–Zhu fix in §2.1.4; the Kummer part has the same direction issue as the Dwork part recorded in E68.

**E-RD6-2 — [S19](#source-19), (10.6.3), p. 759 (Numdam scan of Ann. Sci. École Norm. Sup. 31, 1998).** N F = q_y F N. On M_η ⊗ A(y) the connection is N ⊗ dt/t and its pullback along t ↦ t^{q_y} is q_y N ⊗ dt/t, so horizontality of the map induced by F reads N F = q_y F N; Kedlaya, Weil II Proposition 6.4.4, p. 48, writes EF = qFE. The printed relation would make N raise Frobenius weights by 2, whereas Theorem 10.8 (gr^M_i of weight β + i, with N mapping M_i into M_{i−2}) needs N to lower them by 2.

**E-RD6-3 — [S86](#source-86), (1.5.1), p. 11, with the Dwork F-isocrystal of p. 10 (Numdam scan of Compositio Math. 91, 1994).** Both traces carry the factor (−1)^{n−1}. With the Frobenius structure Crew gives the Dwork F-isocrystal on p. 10 (F(1) = exp(πx^p − πx), in the pullback-to-module direction of §1.1) the p-adic side is moreover the sum for ψ^{-1}: (−1)^{n−1} Σ ψ^{-1} ∘ Tr(x_1 + ⋯ + x_n), which is the ℓ-adic trace for ψ_ℓ^{-1}. For even n the sums for ψ and ψ^{-1} agree; for odd n the sum for ψ^{-1} at a is the sum for ψ at −a. Only H^{n−1}_c of the fibre G_m^{n−1} is nonzero, so the Lefschetz trace formula gives the sign (−1)^{n−1} (for n = 2 the trace is −Σ_x ψ(x + a/x)). The q-power multiplier of Crew's L_ψ is exp(π(x^q − x)) = ∏_{i<s} θ(x^{p^i})^{-1} with θ(t) = exp(π(t − t^p)), and Dwork's identity ∏_{j<s} θ(x̃^{p^j}) = θ(1)^{Tr x}, θ(1) = ψ(1) ≡ 1 + π, gives the trace ψ(Tr x)^{-1} of L_ψ at x (RD.6/dwork-kummer-sign-dictionary (ii)).

**E-RD6-4 — [S5](#source-5), Proof of Theorem 4.4.1, pp. 33-34, arXiv:math/0210149v3.** Both sides decrease by rank(E). Removing a rational point x adds rank(E) to dim H^1_rig (the residues at x) and lowers χ(C/K, O_C) by 1, while Swan_x(E) = 0; for E = O and C = A^1, χ(A^1) = 1 and χ(G_m) = 0. The argument only needs the two changes to be equal.

**E701 — [S98](#source-98), item for the journal's page 331, line 8, p. 1 of the errata note (13 October 2003); read against Lemma 3 of arXiv v2, p. 5.** With Lemma 3's own m the multiplier must be p^{⌊log_p(d(2m + 3) − 2)⌋}, i.e. p^{⌊log_p((2g + 1)(e + 2) − 2)⌋} for F(x)y^e dx with e odd (Harvey §4; Edixhoven Lemma 4.3.5 with even exponent m' = 2m + 2 in the form a·y^{m'}dx/y). The errata formula d(m + 1) − 2 is right only if m is read as Edixhoven's even exponent. For Q = x^3 + x + 1, p = 5 (good reduction, discriminant −31) and m = 0, the reduction of y dx = Q dx/y is (2/5)x dx/y + (3/5) dx/y + d((2/5)xy), computed exactly; it needs the factor 5 = 5^{⌊log_5 7⌋}, while d(m + 1) − 2 = 1 gives 5^0 = 1.

**E702 — [S98](#source-98), paragraph on the integral basis, p. 1 of the errata note.** The span is over 0 ≤ i ≤ 2g − 1 (2g forms, a basis of H^1(A; K)^−), as in Edixhoven's Proposition 5.3.1. H^1(A; K)^− has dimension 2g; the printed index range has only 2g − 1 elements and would miss dx/y, the invariant differential of an elliptic curve when g = 1.

**E703 — [S99](#source-99), proof of Lemma 4.3.5, p. 14 (version of 25 October 2006).** v_∞(y) = −d (d = deg Q = 2g + 1), since y^2 = Q and v_∞(x) = −2. 2v_∞(y) = v_∞(Q) = d·v_∞(x) = −2d; the next values in the proof, v_∞(dx/y) = d − 3 and v_∞(f) ≥ −md − d + 2, use v_∞(y) = −d, so the bound is unaffected.

**E704 — [S101](#source-101), Assumption 1, condition (3), p. 3 (arXiv v2 and the journal version).** Require unit discriminants only for their reduced parts (quotients by the nilradical). The printed condition is sufficient but excludes every ramified map x, for example every hyperelliptic model y^2 = f(x): R^0/(r) = (Z_q[x]/(f))[y]/(y^2) is not reduced, so its discriminant is 0.

**E705 — [S96](#source-96), proof of Lemma 27.10, p. 158 (version 2.21, 22 March 2013).** Every |c_i|_ℓ is at most 1, which is what the first sentence of the proof sets out to show and what integrality of h needs. The argument excludes only |c_i|_ℓ > 1. Equality occurs: f = 1/(1 − t) is in 1 + tZ_ℓ[[t]] with h = 1 − t and c = 1.

**E706 — [S96](#source-96), Summary 27.14(c) and the paragraph proving it, p. 159 (version 2.21, 22 March 2013).** Pairwise coprimality gives only that the coefficients of P_{r,ℓ} are algebraic integers lying in Q_ℓ. Rationality, and with it integrality, needs the multiset of reciprocal roots of each P_{r,ℓ} to be Gal(Q̄/Q)-stable. Purity, the hypothesis of (d), supplies this, as in Deligne, Weil I, p. 277, and RD.7/weight-separated-factor-extraction. State (c) with the conclusion 'coefficients integral over Z', or assume the hypothesis of (d). Two conjugate quadratic algebraic integers α, ᾱ in Q_ℓ can be split as P_1 = 1 − αt and P_3 = 1 − ᾱt. The two factors are coprime and their product is in 1 + tZ[t], but neither factor is in Q[t]. So algebraic-integer reciprocal roots do not put an individual factor in Z[t] without a rationality argument.

**E707 — [S101](#source-101), §4.3 Step III, p. 12, against the proof of Proposition 4.7, p. 14 (arXiv v2).** The two do not match. In the column convention the matrix of F_p^n is F·F^{σ}⋯F^{σ^{n−1}}; the product F^{σ^{n−1}}⋯F is the matrix of F_p^n in the row convention F_p(ω_i) = Σ_j F_{i,j}ω_j. The author's Magma implementation (pcc_q, zeta_q.m, functions frobmatrix and galois_norm) uses rows with the decreasing product, so read F_{i,j} in Step III. For a σ-semilinear map a with column matrix A, a^2 has column matrix A·σ(A). For n = 3 the two orders give different characteristic polynomials: over W(F_8), F_8 = F_2[a]/(a^3 + a + 1), any lift of the matrix with rows (0, 1) and (a, a^2) has trace of A^{σ^2}A^{σ}A ≡ 0 and trace of A·A^{σ}·A^{σ^2} ≡ 1 modulo 2 (computed by hand and by machine).
